cards.a: Deficiencies of iron, vitamin B12, calcium and vitamin D, because malabsorptive surgery reduces absorption. She needs supplementation and monitoring, and pregnancy should be delayed at least 12 to 18 months after surgery.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a history of bariatric surgery. What nutritional issue is most important to monitor?

cards.a: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. It causes intense pruritus without a rash and raised bile acids, and raises the risk of stillbirth, so delivery is usually planned at 37 weeks and ursodeoxycholic acid relieves the itching.
cards.q: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks has itching on her palms and soles, worse at night, with raised bile acids. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Ursodeoxycholic acid to relieve itching and lower bile acids, with delivery planned around 37 weeks. The stillbirth risk rises after 37 weeks, so early delivery is recommended even though the mother feels better.
cards.q: What is the treatment for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, and when is delivery planned?

cards.a: Gestational thrombocytopenia, the most common cause of low platelets in pregnancy. It is mild, appears late in pregnancy, and does not cause bleeding or affect the baby, unlike immune thrombocytopenia or HELLP syndrome.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a platelet count of 90,000 with no other abnormalities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild (usually above 70,000), appears in the third trimester, and has no prior history of low platelets. ITP often appears earlier, can be severe, and may have a history of bruising or low platelets before pregnancy.
cards.q: How can gestational thrombocytopenia be distinguished from immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) in pregnancy?

cards.a: HELLP syndrome — haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets, a severe form of pre-eclampsia. It needs urgent hospital care, blood pressure control, magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention, and delivery.
cards.q: A pregnant woman at 34 weeks has hypertension, headache, epigastric pain and platelets of 85,000 with raised liver enzymes. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Hepatitis B vaccine plus hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth. This combination prevents transmission of hepatitis B during delivery in over 90% of cases.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a positive hepatitis B surface antigen. What should her newborn receive at birth?

cards.a: Azithromycin 1 g as a single dose. Untreated chlamydia raises the risk of preterm birth, and the baby can develop conjunctivitis and pneumonia during vaginal delivery.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has active genital chlamydia. What is the treatment, and why treat it?

cards.a: Metronidazole or clindamycin. Bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy is linked to preterm rupture of membranes and preterm birth, so symptomatic women are treated.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has bacterial vaginosis with a fishy discharge. What is the treatment, and why does it matter?

cards.a: Consider vaginal progesterone, which reduces the risk of preterm birth in women with a short cervix. Cervical cerclage is an option if there is a history of cervical insufficiency or the cervix shortens further.
cards.q: A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has a short cervix of 18 mm on ultrasound and a history of preterm birth. What is the next best step?

cards.a: To speed up fetal lung maturity and reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and death. They are given when preterm birth is expected between 24 and 34 weeks, ideally at least 48 hours before delivery.
cards.q: What is the purpose of giving antenatal corticosteroids before a preterm delivery?

cards.a: About 50% if the partner is heterozygous, and 100% if he is homozygous. Because the risk is real either way, anti-D is given at 28 weeks and after delivery regardless of the partner's exact genotype.
cards.q: A pregnant woman is Rh-negative, 28 weeks, and her partner is Rh-positive. What is the chance the baby is Rh-positive?

cards.a: Yes — moderate exercise such as walking and swimming for about 30 minutes most days is safe and recommended in uncomplicated pregnancy. It reduces the risk of gestational diabetes and excessive weight gain, and should be stopped if there is bleeding, pain or contractions.
cards.q: A pregnant woman asks whether she can exercise during pregnancy. What is the advice?

cards.a: Low molecular weight heparin, which does not cross the placenta and is safe for the fetus. Warfarin is avoided, and treatment continues through pregnancy and for at least 6 weeks after delivery.
cards.q: A pregnant woman develops a deep vein thrombosis. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Clotting factors rise, fibrinogen increases, and protein S falls, while venous stasis develops from the uterus pressing on pelvic veins. This protects against bleeding at delivery but raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
cards.q: Why is pregnancy a hypercoagulable state?

cards.a: Prophylactic low molecular weight heparin throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum. Her risk of recurrence is high, and heparin is safe in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta.
cards.q: A pregnant woman has a history of a previous blood clot. What prophylaxis should she receive?

cards.a: Blood loss of 500 mL or more after a vaginal delivery, or 1000 mL or more after a caesarean delivery. Any amount that causes haemodynamic instability also counts, because a woman can bleed dangerously before reaching the textbook number, especially if she was anaemic before delivery.
cards.q: What is the definition of postpartum haemorrhage after a vaginal delivery, and after a caesarean delivery?

cards.a: Tone (uterine atony), Trauma (lacerations, uterine rupture or inversion), Tissue (retained placenta or membranes), and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Atony is the most common cause, so the first step is always to check whether the uterus is firm or boggy.
cards.q: What are the 4 Ts that cause postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Uterine atony. The first step is firm bimanual uterine massage together with oxytocin, because a contracted uterus compresses the spiral arteries in the placental bed and stops the bleeding mechanically.
cards.q: A woman bleeds heavily minutes after delivery and her uterus feels soft and boggy on examination. What is the most likely cause and the first step?

cards.a: Oxytocin, given IV or IM. It causes rhythmic uterine contractions that compress the bleeding vessels, and it works within minutes with the fewest side effects of all the uterotonics.
cards.q: What is the first-line uterotonic drug for postpartum haemorrhage caused by uterine atony?

cards.a: Methylergonovine (methergine), given IM. It causes sustained tetanic uterine contraction. It must be avoided in hypertension and preeclampsia because it is a potent vasoconstrictor and can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure.
cards.q: What is the second-line uterotonic if oxytocin fails to control postpartum bleeding?

cards.a: Carboprost (15-methyl prostaglandin F2-alpha, Hemabate). It can cause bronchospasm, so it is avoided in asthma. It is also avoided in active cardiac, pulmonary, renal or hepatic disease.
cards.q: Which uterotonic is contraindicated in a woman with asthma, and why?

cards.a: Methylergonovine (methergine). It causes vasoconstriction and can sharply raise blood pressure, which is dangerous in a woman who already has hypertension or preeclampsia.
cards.q: Which uterotonic is contraindicated in a woman with hypertension or preeclampsia, and why?

cards.a: First oxytocin, then methylergonovine (if no hypertension), then carboprost (if no asthma), then misoprostol (prostaglandin E1, rectal or oral). Each drug works by a different mechanism, so adding a second or third drug can succeed where one alone failed.
cards.q: What is the order of uterotonic drugs for postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony?

cards.a: Avoid carboprost because it can trigger bronchospasm in asthma. Misoprostol is a reasonable next choice, because it does not cause bronchospasm and can be given rectally even when IV access is limited.
cards.q: A woman continues to bleed after oxytocin and methylergonovine. She has asthma. Which uterotonic should be avoided and which can be used instead?

cards.a: An intrauterine balloon tamponade device placed inside the uterus and inflated with saline. It presses directly on the bleeding placental bed. It is used when uterotonics fail, as a temporising measure before surgery.
cards.q: What is a Bakri balloon and when is it used in postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Uterine artery ligation, B-Lynch compression sutures, and finally hysterectomy as a last resort. Surgery is escalated quickly because ongoing bleeding leads to coagulopathy, which makes every later step harder.
cards.q: What surgical steps are used when medical treatment and balloon tamponade fail to stop postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: A genital tract laceration, especially of the cervix or vagina. A firm uterus rules out atony, so the bleeding must come from trauma; a careful speculum examination is needed because cervical tears can bleed heavily and are easily missed.
cards.q: A woman has heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery, the uterus is firm and well contracted, and no retained tissue is felt. What should be looked for next?

cards.a: Continued bleeding after delivery with a uterus that does not contract well, and a missing cotyledon or ragged membranes on inspection of the delivered placenta. Retained tissue prevents the uterus from contracting fully, so manual removal of the placenta is required.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a retained placenta causing postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Overdistension of the uterus (twins, polyhydramnios, large baby), prolonged labour, oxytocin use during labour, chorioamnionitis, and a history of prior atony. An overstretched or exhausted uterus contracts poorly after delivery.
cards.q: Which risk factors make uterine atony more likely?

cards.a: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) from massive blood loss and consumption of clotting factors. Give blood products, including fresh frozen plasma and platelets, and correct the underlying bleeding, because replacing volume with crystalloid alone worsens the coagulopathy.
cards.q: A woman with postpartum haemorrhage develops oozing from IV sites and her blood does not clot. What is happening and what is the next step?

cards.a: Packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets, often in a 1:1:1 ratio. This replaces red cells, clotting factors and platelets together, mimicking whole blood and preventing dilutional coagulopathy.
cards.q: What blood products are given in massive postpartum haemorrhage, and in what ratio?

cards.a: It is an antifibrinolytic that stabilises clot by blocking plasmin. It is given early, within 3 hours of bleeding onset, in addition to uterotonics, because it reduces death from bleeding when given promptly.
cards.q: What is the role of tranexamic acid in postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Secondary (late) postpartum haemorrhage, most often from retained products of conception or endometritis. Unlike early haemorrhage, which is usually atony, late bleeding points to tissue left in the uterus or infection preventing proper involution.
cards.q: A woman bleeds heavily 2 weeks after delivery. What is the most likely cause?

cards.a: Pelvic ultrasound to look for retained products of conception, plus examination for infection and a pregnancy test to exclude a new pregnancy. Ultrasound guides whether curettage is needed, and infection must be treated with antibiotics first if present.
cards.q: What is the workup for secondary postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Uterine inversion. The uterus has turned inside out and prolapsed through the cervix, usually from excessive cord traction on a fundally implanted placenta. It is an emergency: replace the uterus manually and give uterotonics once it is back in place.
cards.q: A woman has sudden severe abdominal pain, shock and vaginal bleeding after a vaginal delivery. The uterus cannot be felt on abdominal examination. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. It usually appears 2 to 3 days after delivery and is caused by polymicrobial infection of the decidua, most often after caesarean delivery or prolonged rupture of membranes.
cards.q: What is the classic triad of postpartum endometritis?

cards.a: Polymicrobial, with a mix of aerobes and anaerobes, including group B streptococcus, E. coli, anaerobes and chlamydia. This is why treatment uses broad-spectrum antibiotics rather than a single narrow agent.
cards.q: What is the most common organism pattern in postpartum endometritis?

cards.a: Clindamycin plus gentamicin. Clindamycin covers anaerobes and gram-positive organisms, gentamicin covers gram-negatives, and together they cover the usual polymicrobial mix. Ampicillin is added if enterococcus is suspected.
cards.q: What is the first-line antibiotic regimen for postpartum endometritis?

cards.a: Postpartum endometritis. Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (clindamycin plus gentamicin) and examine for retained products or a wound infection, because delay allows the infection to spread to the parametrium or bloodstream.
cards.q: A woman 3 days after caesarean delivery has fever, lower abdominal pain and foul lochia. Her white cell count is raised. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Caesarean delivery, especially after prolonged labour or prolonged rupture of membranes. The surgical incision and the open cervix give bacteria direct access to the uterus, so prophylactic antibiotics are given at caesarean.
cards.q: What is the most important risk factor for postpartum endometritis?

cards.a: A pelvic abscess, septic pelvic thrombophlebitis, or retained products of conception. Failure to improve means the infection is not simply endometritis, so imaging (ultrasound or CT) is needed to find a collection or clot that antibiotics alone cannot clear.
cards.q: A woman with endometritis does not improve after 48 to 72 hours of antibiotics. What should be considered next?

cards.a: Infected clot in the ovarian or pelvic veins, presenting as persistent spiking fevers despite antibiotics in a woman recently treated for endometritis, often with few localising signs. It is diagnosed by CT or MRI and treated with anticoagulation plus antibiotics.
cards.q: What is septic pelvic thrombophlebitis and how does it present?

cards.a: Lochia rubra is red and bloody for the first 3 to 4 days, lochia serosa is pink-brown for about 10 days, and lochia alba is white-yellow for up to 6 weeks. A return to bright red bleeding after it had lightened suggests retained tissue or infection.
cards.q: What distinguishes lochia rubra, serosa and alba?

cards.a: Normal lochia can smell unpleasant and a low-grade fever can occur in the first 24 hours after delivery, but foul discharge with fever after day 2 still warrants evaluation for endometritis. The absence of tenderness makes endometritis less likely, so also consider a urinary tract infection or wound infection.
cards.q: A woman 5 days after delivery has fever and a foul vaginal discharge, but her uterus is not tender and her white cell count is normal. What else could explain this?

cards.a: Erythema, warmth, swelling, pain and purulent discharge at the incision, usually 4 to 7 days after surgery, often with fever. It is most often caused by skin flora such as Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
cards.q: What are the signs of a caesarean wound infection?

cards.a: Open the wound, drain any pus, clean it, and give antibiotics covering skin flora. Superficial infections heal by secondary intention, because closing an infected wound traps bacteria inside.
cards.q: What is the treatment for a superficial caesarean wound infection without fascial involvement?

cards.a: Fascial dehiscence or necrotising fasciitis. Separation of the fascia means the abdominal wall has lost its strength, and necrotising infection can spread rapidly, so urgent surgical exploration is needed.
cards.q: A woman 6 days after caesarean has fever, wound discharge and the wound edges separate easily. What is the feared complication?

cards.a: Dehiscence is separation of the wound layers, usually skin and subcutaneous tissue; evisceration is protrusion of bowel or other organs through the wound. Evisceration is a surgical emergency requiring immediate covering with sterile saline dressings and urgent repair.
cards.q: What is the difference between wound dehiscence and wound evisceration?

cards.a: Women with obesity, diabetes, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, or prolonged surgery. Obesity and diabetes impair wound healing and blood supply, while infection at the time of surgery seeds the wound.
cards.q: Which patients are at highest risk of caesarean wound infection and dehiscence?

cards.a: A single dose of a first-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin given before the skin incision reduces wound infection and endometritis. Giving it before the incision, rather than after cord clamping, gives the best tissue levels at the time of bacterial contamination.
cards.q: What is the role of prophylactic antibiotics at caesarean delivery?

cards.a: Perineal haematoma or abscess. A haematoma forms from bleeding into the perineal tissues after a laceration or episiotomy; if it becomes infected it forms an abscess. Large or expanding haematomas need drainage, and an abscess needs incision and drainage plus antibiotics.
cards.q: A woman after vaginal delivery has severe perineal pain, swelling and fever. Examination shows a tense, tender, fluctuant mass in the perineum. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Observation, ice packs, analgesia and close monitoring. Small haematomas usually reabsorb on their own, and surgery is reserved for expanding, large or infected collections because operating on a small stable one can cause more bleeding.
cards.q: What is the management of a small stable perineal haematoma after delivery?

cards.a: Inflammation of the breast tissue, usually 2 to 3 weeks after delivery in a breastfeeding woman, caused by milk stasis with secondary infection, most often Staphylococcus aureus. It presents with a painful, red, swollen area of one breast plus fever and flu-like symptoms.
cards.q: What is mastitis and when does it usually occur?

cards.a: Dicloxacillin or cephalexin, which cover Staphylococcus aureus including penicillinase-producing strains. Treatment is given for 10 to 14 days, and the woman should continue breastfeeding, because emptying the breast is part of the treatment.
cards.q: What is the first-line antibiotic for mastitis?

cards.a: No, she should continue breastfeeding or pumping from the affected breast. Continued emptying relieves milk stasis, which is the root cause, and the baby is not harmed by the milk because the infection is in the breast tissue, not a systemic infection of the milk.
cards.q: Should a woman with mastitis stop breastfeeding from the affected breast?

cards.a: Frequent and complete emptying of the breast by breastfeeding or pumping, plus supportive measures such as warm compresses and analgesia. Antibiotics alone fail if milk stasis persists, because stagnant milk keeps feeding the inflammation.
cards.q: What is the most important non-antibiotic treatment for mastitis?

cards.a: Ultrasound of the breast to look for a breast abscess. An abscess is a walled-off collection of pus that antibiotics cannot penetrate, so it needs needle aspiration or surgical drainage.
cards.q: A woman with mastitis has a persistent painful lump that does not improve after 48 hours of antibiotics. What is the next step?

cards.a: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, repeated if needed, plus antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus. Surgical incision and drainage is reserved for large, multiloculated or recurrent abscesses, because aspiration preserves breastfeeding and leaves a smaller scar.
cards.q: What is the treatment for a breast abscess in a breastfeeding woman?

cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus, entering through a cracked nipple. It is the classic cause of infectious mastitis, which is why first-line antibiotics are chosen to cover it.
cards.q: A breastfeeding woman has a painful red wedge-shaped area of the breast with fever. What organism is most likely?

cards.a: Engorgement is bilateral, painful fullness of both breasts from milk accumulation, usually 3 to 5 days after delivery, without fever or a focal red area. Mastitis is usually unilateral, with a focal red tender area, fever and systemic symptoms, indicating infection.
cards.q: What is the difference between breast engorgement and mastitis?

cards.a: Frequent breastfeeding, warm compresses before feeds, cold compresses after feeds, and analgesia. Engorgement resolves as milk supply and demand balance out; it is not treated with antibiotics because there is no infection.
cards.q: What is the treatment for breast engorgement?

cards.a: Poor latch causing nipple trauma. The key intervention is correcting the latch with lactation support, because a good latch prevents further trauma and allows effective milk transfer; topical lanolin alone does not fix the underlying problem.
cards.q: A woman has a cracked, painful nipple and her baby is not latching well. What is the most likely cause and the key intervention?

cards.a: A tender, localised lump in one breast without fever or systemic illness. It is caused by milk stasis in a single duct and is treated with frequent feeding, massage and warm compresses; fever and spreading redness would suggest progression to mastitis.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of a plugged milk duct?

cards.a: A 10-item self-report questionnaire used to screen for postpartum depression. A score of 10 or more suggests possible depression and warrants further evaluation. It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, so a high score must be followed by a clinical interview.
cards.q: What is the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) and what is it used for?

cards.a: Within the first 2 to 3 months after delivery, though it can begin any time in the first year. This is why screening is done at the postpartum visit and at well-baby visits, not only in the first days after birth.
cards.q: When is the peak onset of postpartum depression?

cards.a: Postpartum blues affects up to half of new mothers, starts 2 to 3 days after delivery, and resolves within 2 weeks, with mood lability, tearfulness and anxiety but no functional impairment. Postpartum depression lasts longer than 2 weeks, causes persistent low mood, anhedonia and impaired functioning, and needs treatment.
cards.q: What is the difference between postpartum blues and postpartum depression?

cards.a: Sertraline. It is preferred because it has the lowest transfer into breast milk of the SSRIs and the most safety data in breastfeeding, so the infant exposure is minimal.
cards.q: What is the first-line antidepressant for postpartum depression in a breastfeeding woman?

cards.a: Sertraline and its metabolite are present in very low levels in breast milk and are usually undetectable in the infant's blood. Other SSRIs such as fluoxetine have longer half-lives and higher infant exposure, so sertraline is the safest first choice.
cards.q: Why is sertraline preferred over other SSRIs in breastfeeding mothers?

cards.a: No. The benefits of breastfeeding and of treating her depression outweigh the minimal infant exposure to sertraline. Stopping breastfeeding would remove a protective factor and add guilt, worsening her mood.
cards.q: A breastfeeding woman with postpartum depression is started on sertraline. Should she stop breastfeeding?

cards.a: A psychiatric emergency with delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking and confusion, usually within the first 2 weeks after delivery, most often in women with a history of bipolar disorder. It carries a high risk of suicide and infanticide, so it needs urgent hospital admission.
cards.q: What is postpartum psychosis and when does it usually present?

cards.a: Postpartum psychosis. Admit her urgently to hospital, ensure the baby's safety with supervised care, and start antipsychotic treatment with psychiatric input. This is a medical emergency, not something to manage with reassurance and follow-up.
cards.q: A woman 1 week after delivery believes the baby is possessed, hears voices telling her to harm the baby, and is agitated and confused. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Women with a history of bipolar disorder or a previous episode of postpartum psychosis. The risk is highest in the first 2 weeks after delivery, so these women need close monitoring and a clear safety plan before discharge.
cards.q: Which women are at highest risk of postpartum psychosis?

cards.a: Urgent inpatient psychiatric admission, antipsychotics, and often mood stabilisers such as lithium, with electroconvulsive therapy for severe or refractory cases. Safety of mother and baby comes first, and breastfeeding is usually paused during acute treatment.
cards.q: What is the treatment for postpartum psychosis?

cards.a: Postpartum depression. Screen with the EPDS, confirm with a clinical interview, assess for suicidal thoughts and safety, then start treatment with psychotherapy and an SSRI such as sertraline. Early treatment improves outcomes for both mother and baby.
cards.q: A woman 4 weeks after delivery has persistent sadness, insomnia, guilt and difficulty bonding with her baby. What is the diagnosis and the first step?

cards.a: Many women do not volunteer their symptoms because of stigma or guilt, and untreated depression impairs bonding, breastfeeding and the child's development. Routine screening catches cases that would otherwise be missed.
cards.q: Why is screening for postpartum depression important even when the mother seems well?

cards.a: Pulmonary embolism. Pregnancy and the postpartum period are hypercoagulable, venous stasis is common, and a clot from the leg veins can travel to the lungs, so sudden dyspnoea, chest pain and tachycardia after delivery must be taken seriously.
cards.q: What is the most common cause of maternal death from venous thromboembolism in the postpartum period?

cards.a: Deep vein thrombosis. Confirm with compression duplex ultrasound of the leg veins and start anticoagulation promptly, because an untreated clot can embolise to the lungs.
cards.q: A woman 2 weeks after caesarean delivery develops unilateral leg swelling, calf pain and warmth. What is the most likely diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Low molecular weight heparin, such as enoxaparin. It does not cross into breast milk in significant amounts and does not require monitoring, whereas warfarin needs INR monitoring and direct oral anticoagulants have limited safety data in breastfeeding.
cards.q: What is the anticoagulant of choice for treating venous thromboembolism in a breastfeeding woman?

cards.a: Pulmonary embolism. Start anticoagulation with heparin immediately if there is no contraindication, and confirm with CT pulmonary angiography. Do not wait for imaging if clinical suspicion is high, because delay can be fatal.
cards.q: A woman 10 days after delivery develops sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and low oxygen saturation. What is the most likely diagnosis and the immediate step?

cards.a: Women with a prior venous thromboembolism, thrombophilia, or multiple risk factors such as caesarean delivery combined with obesity, immobility or preeclampsia. Risk assessment is done before discharge, because the postpartum period is the highest-risk time for clots.
cards.q: Which postpartum women need pharmacological thromboprophylaxis?

cards.a: Early mobilisation, compression stockings and sequential compression devices during and after caesarean delivery. Movement and compression reduce venous stasis, which is one of the three factors in Virchow's triad driving clot formation.
cards.q: What mechanical measures help prevent postpartum venous thromboembolism?

cards.a: At least 3 months, including at least 6 weeks postpartum. This covers the period of highest risk, because the hypercoagulable state of pregnancy takes weeks to resolve after delivery.
cards.q: What is the duration of anticoagulation for a postpartum deep vein thrombosis?

cards.a: Inflammation of the thyroid gland in the first year after delivery, caused by an autoimmune reaction as the immune system rebounds after pregnancy. It typically starts with a hyperthyroid phase at 1 to 4 months, followed by a hypothyroid phase at 4 to 8 months.
cards.q: What is postpartum thyroiditis and when does it typically occur?

cards.a: Postpartum thyroiditis in its hyperthyroid phase. It is caused by release of stored thyroid hormone from an inflamed gland, not by overproduction, so it is usually self-limited and treated symptomatically with beta blockers.
cards.q: A woman 3 months after delivery has palpitations, weight loss, tremor and heat intolerance. Her TSH is low and her free T4 is high. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Postpartum thyroiditis is painless, self-limited, has low radioactive iodine uptake because the gland is leaking hormone rather than making it, and usually resolves. Graves disease causes sustained overproduction with high uptake and needs antithyroid drugs.
cards.q: How is the hyperthyroid phase of postpartum thyroiditis different from Graves disease?

cards.a: Postpartum thyroiditis in its hypothyroid phase. The inflamed gland can no longer make enough hormone, so thyroid replacement with levothyroxine is needed if symptoms are significant or the TSH is very high.
cards.q: A woman 6 months after delivery has fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation. Her TSH is high and her free T4 is low. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: No. Antithyroid drugs block new hormone synthesis, but postpartum thyroiditis releases preformed hormone from a damaged gland, so they do not help. Beta blockers control the symptoms while the phase resolves on its own.
cards.q: Should the hyperthyroid phase of postpartum thyroiditis be treated with methimazole?

cards.a: About one in five women develops permanent hypothyroidism, and the condition recurs in most subsequent pregnancies. Annual thyroid function testing is recommended, because permanent failure can develop years later.
cards.q: What is the long-term risk after an episode of postpartum thyroiditis?

cards.a: Women with type 1 diabetes or pre-existing thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO positive). The autoimmune background makes the postpartum immune rebound more likely to attack the thyroid.
cards.q: Which women are at highest risk of postpartum thyroiditis?

cards.a: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, then continued breastfeeding with complementary foods up to 2 years or beyond. Breast milk provides optimal nutrition and immune protection, and exclusive breastfeeding delays the return of fertility.
cards.q: What is the recommended duration of exclusive breastfeeding?

cards.a: Breastfeeding as contraception, effective only if all three are true: the baby is under 6 months old, the mother is exclusively breastfeeding (including at night), and her periods have not returned. If any criterion fails, another method is needed.
cards.q: What is the lactational amenorrhoea method of contraception, and what are its three criteria?

cards.a: Progestin-only methods, such as the progestin-only pill, depot medroxyprogesterone, the implant and the hormonal IUD. Combined oestrogen-containing methods are avoided in the first 6 weeks because oestrogen can reduce milk supply.
cards.q: A breastfeeding woman asks about contraception. Which hormonal methods are safe while breastfeeding?

cards.a: Oestrogen can suppress milk production, and the early postpartum period is already the highest-risk time for venous thromboembolism, which oestrogen further increases. After 6 weeks, combined methods can be considered if the woman is not breastfeeding.
cards.q: Why are combined oral contraceptives avoided in the first 6 weeks postpartum?

cards.a: Within 10 minutes of placental delivery, or at the 6-week postpartum visit. Insertion between 10 minutes and 4 weeks is avoided because the expulsion rate is higher and the perforation risk is greater while the uterus is still involuting.
cards.q: When can an intrauterine device be inserted after delivery?

cards.a: A long-acting reversible method, such as an intrauterine device or the contraceptive implant. They are more than 99 percent effective, do not depend on daily adherence, and are safe in breastfeeding.
cards.q: What is the most effective reversible contraception for a postpartum woman?

cards.a: Immediately after a vaginal delivery (postpartum tubal ligation, usually within 24 to 48 hours) or at the time of caesarean delivery. It should only be done after informed consent, because it is intended to be permanent and regret is more common in younger women.
cards.q: A woman wants permanent contraception after delivery. When can tubal ligation be done?

cards.a: When she feels ready and any perineal or caesarean wound has healed, usually after 4 to 6 weeks. There is no strict medical deadline, but contraception should be discussed before resuming, because ovulation can return before the first period, especially if she is not breastfeeding.
cards.q: When can a woman safely resume sexual intercourse after delivery?

cards.a: New-onset hypertension with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction developing after delivery, usually within the first week but up to 6 weeks postpartum. It can occur even in women who had no hypertension during pregnancy, so postpartum headaches and swelling must not be dismissed.
cards.q: What is postpartum preeclampsia and when does it present?

cards.a: Postpartum preeclampsia with severe features. Admit her, control the blood pressure, give magnesium sulfate to prevent seizures, and monitor closely, because postpartum eclampsia can occur even after a normal pregnancy and delivery.
cards.q: A woman 5 days after delivery has a headache, blurred vision, blood pressure 160 over 110, and protein in her urine. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, antihypertensives such as labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine, and close monitoring. Delivery has already occurred, so treatment focuses on preventing seizures, stroke and organ damage.
cards.q: What is the treatment for postpartum preeclampsia with severe features?

cards.a: Postpartum eclampsia. Seizures after delivery in a woman with new hypertension and proteinuria are eclampsia until proven otherwise, and magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment.
cards.q: A woman 3 days after delivery has a seizure. She had normal blood pressure throughout pregnancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Magnesium sulfate, given IV. It reduces the risk of recurrent seizures more effectively than other anticonvulsants and also has a mild antihypertensive effect.
cards.q: What is the first-line drug for preventing and treating eclamptic seizures?

cards.a: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression, and cardiac arrest at very high levels. The antidote is calcium gluconate, and magnesium levels, reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output must be monitored during the infusion.
cards.q: What are the signs of magnesium sulfate toxicity?

cards.a: Blood pressure usually normalises within days to weeks after delivery, but it should be checked before discharge and again within the first week, with follow-up until it is normal. Persistent hypertension beyond 12 weeks is reclassified as chronic hypertension.
cards.q: A woman with preeclampsia during pregnancy asks how long her blood pressure will be monitored after delivery. What is the answer?

cards.a: Delivery removes the placenta, which drives preeclampsia, but the vascular and endothelial damage takes time to resolve, so stroke, seizures and pulmonary oedema can still occur in the first days to weeks after delivery.
cards.q: Why is postpartum hypertension dangerous even though the baby has been delivered?

cards.a: A sustained blood pressure of 150 over 100 or higher, or 160 over 110 in severe disease, requires antihypertensive treatment. Severe hypertension must be treated promptly to prevent stroke, even if the woman feels well.
cards.q: What blood pressure threshold requires treatment in the postpartum period?

cards.a: Blood pressure checks in the first week, review at 6 weeks, and long-term cardiovascular risk counselling, because preeclampsia doubles the later risk of chronic hypertension, heart disease and stroke.
cards.q: What is the recommended follow-up for a woman who had preeclampsia?

cards.a: First degree: skin and vaginal mucosa only. Second degree: perineal muscles. Third degree: anal sphincter complex. Fourth degree: anal sphincter and rectal mucosa. The degree determines the repair technique and the risk of long-term incontinence.
cards.q: What are the four degrees of perineal tears?

cards.a: Faecal incontinence and anal sphincter dysfunction. Careful layered repair and follow-up are essential, because a missed sphincter injury leads to permanent incontinence.
cards.q: What is the most important long-term complication of a third- or fourth-degree perineal tear?

cards.a: In the operating theatre under good anaesthesia, with a layered repair of the rectal mucosa, internal and external anal sphincter, and perineal muscles, plus broad-spectrum antibiotics and laxatives afterwards. Good exposure and a proper sphincter repair are essential for continence.
cards.q: How is a third-degree perineal tear repaired?

cards.a: A surgical cut in the perineum to enlarge the vaginal opening. Routine episiotomy is no longer recommended; it is used selectively, for example for an instrumental delivery or fetal distress, because routine use increases the risk of severe tears.
cards.q: What is the role of an episiotomy and when is it used now?

cards.a: Postpartum urinary retention. It is usually caused by perineal pain, swelling or epidural anaesthesia. The next step is bladder catheterisation to empty the bladder and prevent overdistension injury.
cards.q: A woman after delivery cannot pass urine and has lower abdominal pain and a palpable bladder. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Perineal oedema and pain, epidural or spinal anaesthesia, a long labour, or an instrumental delivery. The bladder becomes overdistended and the detrusor muscle loses its ability to contract, so early recognition and catheterisation prevent permanent damage.
cards.q: What causes postpartum urinary retention?

cards.a: Postpartum urinary tract infection. It is common after catheterisation during labour or caesarean delivery, and it is treated with antibiotics safe in breastfeeding, such as nitrofurantoin or cephalexin, after a urine culture.
cards.q: A woman has burning on passing urine and urinary frequency 4 days after delivery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Blood pressure, mood and depression screening, breastfeeding, contraception, wound and perineal healing, urinary and bowel function, and return of periods. It is also the time to review any pregnancy complications such as preeclampsia or gestational diabetes and plan long-term follow-up.
cards.q: What should be checked at the 6-week postpartum visit?

cards.a: A 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test at 6 to 12 weeks postpartum. Gestational diabetes resolves after delivery in most women, but the test identifies those who have persistent diabetes or prediabetes and need ongoing care.
cards.q: A woman who had gestational diabetes asks about follow-up after delivery. What test is recommended and when?

cards.a: It is the main chance to screen for depression, hypertension, diabetes, anaemia and contraceptive needs, and to review complications from pregnancy and delivery. Many problems are silent at this stage, so a structured review catches them before they cause harm.
cards.q: Why is the 6-week postpartum visit important even if the woman feels well?

cards.a: Postpartum pituitary necrosis caused by severe blood loss and hypotension during delivery, which infarcts the enlarged pituitary gland. It leads to hypopituitarism, with failure to lactate, loss of pubic and axillary hair, amenorrhoea and eventually hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency.
cards.q: What is Sheehan syndrome?

cards.a: Sheehan syndrome. The pituitary gland was damaged by hypotension during the haemorrhage, so prolactin, gonadotropins, thyroid-stimulating hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone are all deficient. Treatment is lifelong hormone replacement.
cards.q: A woman had a massive postpartum haemorrhage and now, months later, cannot produce breast milk, has not had a period, and feels constantly tired and cold. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Failure to lactate after delivery. Prolactin deficiency appears first because lactotrophs are the most vulnerable pituitary cells to ischaemia, so a woman who cannot produce milk after a major haemorrhage should be investigated for Sheehan syndrome.
cards.q: What is the first sign of Sheehan syndrome?

cards.a: Heart failure from left ventricular systolic dysfunction developing in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months after delivery, without another cause. It presents with dyspnoea, orthopnoea, leg swelling and fatigue, and is diagnosed by echocardiography showing a reduced ejection fraction.
cards.q: What is postpartum cardiomyopathy?

cards.a: Postpartum cardiomyopathy. The key test is an echocardiogram, which shows a dilated left ventricle with a reduced ejection fraction. It is easily mistaken for normal postpartum tiredness, so a high index of suspicion is needed.
cards.q: A woman 3 weeks after delivery has progressive shortness of breath, orthopnoea, swollen legs and a raised jugular venous pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis and the key test?

cards.a: Standard heart failure treatment with diuretics, beta blockers and ACE inhibitors, with anticoagulation if the ejection fraction is very low because of the risk of intracardiac clot. Bromocriptine is sometimes added in specialist care. Many women recover, but a subsequent pregnancy carries high risk.
cards.q: What is the treatment for postpartum cardiomyopathy?

cards.a: Resuscitation with large-bore IV access, oxygen, blood products and uterotonics together, not one after another. She is in haemorrhagic shock, so restoring circulating volume and stopping the bleeding must happen at the same time, with early calls for senior help.
cards.q: A woman is 2 days after delivery and has heavy bleeding, a boggy uterus and a blood pressure of 90 over 60 with a heart rate of 120. What is the immediate priority?

cards.a: Active management of the third stage: oxytocin contracts the uterus, speeds placental delivery and reduces blood loss. It is the single most effective step in preventing postpartum haemorrhage.
cards.q: Why is oxytocin given routinely after delivery of the baby?

cards.a: Primary haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours of delivery and is usually caused by atony, trauma, retained tissue or coagulopathy. Secondary haemorrhage occurs from 24 hours to 12 weeks after delivery and is usually caused by retained products or endometritis.
cards.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary postpartum haemorrhage?

cards.a: Endometritis. The clean wound makes a wound infection unlikely, and the triad of fever, uterine tenderness and foul lochia points to infection of the uterine cavity.
cards.q: A woman after caesarean delivery has fever on day 2, a tender uterus and foul lochia. Her wound looks clean. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus. Treatment is wound opening and drainage plus antibiotics covering staphylococci, such as flucloxacillin or cephalexin, with review for deeper fascial involvement.
cards.q: A woman 1 week after delivery has a red, hot, swollen and painful caesarean wound with pus. What organism is most likely and what is the treatment?

cards.a: Clindamycin, which covers Staphylococcus aureus and is safe in breastfeeding. Macrolides such as erythromycin are an alternative, but clindamycin is preferred because of better staphylococcal coverage.
cards.q: A breastfeeding woman has a fever and a painful red breast. She is allergic to penicillin. What antibiotic can be used?

cards.a: Impaired bonding, reduced breastfeeding, and delayed cognitive and emotional development. Treating the mother protects the baby, which is why screening and early treatment are a priority, not an optional extra.
cards.q: What is the risk of untreated postpartum depression for the baby?

cards.a: A postpartum manic episode or emerging postpartum psychosis. The postpartum period is the highest-risk time for relapse in bipolar disorder, so urgent psychiatric assessment is needed, as mania can rapidly progress to psychosis.
cards.q: A woman with a history of bipolar disorder is 1 week postpartum and is sleeping very little, is elated and grandiose, and is making impulsive plans. What is the concern?

cards.a: Fluoxetine. Its long half-life and active metabolite lead to accumulation in the infant, so sertraline or paroxetine are preferred when a breastfeeding mother needs an SSRI.
cards.q: Which antidepressant should be avoided in breastfeeding because of a long half-life and higher infant exposure?

cards.a: A long-acting reversible method such as a copper or hormonal intrauterine device. It is highly effective, safe in breastfeeding, and lasts for years without daily effort.
cards.q: What contraceptive method is best for a breastfeeding woman who wants no more children and does not want surgery?

cards.a: Postpartum thyroiditis in the hyperthyroid phase, driven by autoimmune thyroid damage. Positive anti-TPO antibodies support the diagnosis and predict a higher risk of permanent hypothyroidism.
cards.q: A woman 4 months after delivery has fatigue, palpitations and weight loss. Her thyroid antibodies are positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Treat the severe hypertension urgently with IV labetalol or hydralazine, give magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and monitor in a high-dependency setting. Severe postpartum hypertension can cause stroke within hours.
cards.q: A woman after delivery develops a headache, visual changes and a blood pressure of 170 over 115. What is the immediate management?
A woman with 6 weeks of amenorrhea presents with vaginal bleeding and unilateral pelvic pain. What is the classic triad of ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, and unilateral pelvic (adnexal) pain. Think ectopic pregnancy in any reproductive-age woman with abdominal pain and a positive pregnancy test until proven otherwise, because a ruptured ectopic is a life-threatening emergency.

cards.q: What are the major risk factors for ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Prior ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or tubal damage, prior tubal surgery or sterilisation, assisted reproduction (IVF), smoking, and intrauterine device (IUD) use. All of these damage or distort the fallopian tube so the embryo implants there instead of travelling to the uterus.

cards.q: Where does ectopic pregnancy most commonly implant?
cards.a: The ampulla of the fallopian tube, in over 90% of cases. The ampulla is the widest part of the tube, so the embryo is most likely to get stuck and implant there.

cards.q: A pregnant woman has vaginal bleeding and an empty uterus on transvaginal ultrasound with a beta-hCG of 2500. What does the discriminatory zone mean here?
cards.a: The discriminatory zone is the beta-hCG level (about 1500-2000 mIU/mL with transvaginal ultrasound) above which an intrauterine gestational sac should usually be visible. An empty uterus above this level raises suspicion for ectopic pregnancy, but a single value never proves it, so confirm with serial beta-hCG and repeat imaging.

cards.q: In early pregnancy, what pattern of beta-hCG rise suggests a nonviable or ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: A rise of less than about 53% over 48 hours. In a normal early intrauterine pregnancy beta-hCG roughly doubles every 48 hours, so a slow rise means the pregnancy is not growing normally and may be ectopic or failing.

cards.q: A woman with a known ectopic pregnancy suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, hypotension, and shoulder-tip pain. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood and take her urgently to surgery (laparoscopy or laparotomy). This is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemoperitoneum; shoulder-tip pain (Kehr sign) comes from blood irritating the diaphragm, and she can bleed to death quickly, so do not delay for more imaging.

cards.q: What are the criteria for treating an ectopic pregnancy with methotrexate instead of surgery?
cards.a: Haemodynamically stable, unruptured ectopic, beta-hCG usually under 5000, no fetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, normal liver and kidney function, and a reliable patient who will return for follow-up. Methotrexate only works when the patient is stable and the pregnancy is small.

cards.q: What are the contraindications to methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: Ruptured ectopic or haemodynamic instability, immunodeficiency, active liver or kidney disease, blood dyscrasia, peptic ulcer disease, breastfeeding, and inability to follow up. Methotrexate is a cytotoxic drug that needs a stable patient with healthy organs to clear it safely.

cards.q: How does methotrexate treat an ectopic pregnancy?
cards.a: It is a folate antagonist that blocks dihydrofolate reductase, stopping DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. The trophoblast of the ectopic pregnancy divides rapidly, so it dies and the pregnancy resolves without surgery.

cards.q: A Rh-negative woman is treated for an ectopic pregnancy. What must she receive and why?
cards.a: Anti-D (Rh) immunoglobulin. Any pregnancy event in an Rh-negative woman can expose her to Rh-positive fetal blood and cause her to make anti-D antibodies, which would attack a future Rh-positive baby, so anti-D prevents this sensitisation.

cards.q: Why is heterotopic pregnancy (one intrauterine and one ectopic pregnancy at the same time) more common after IVF?
cards.a: Because more than one embryo is transferred, so one can implant in the uterus and another in the tube. Seeing a normal intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound does not exclude a coexisting ectopic in a woman who had IVF and has pain.

cards.q: Why is an interstitial (cornual) ectopic pregnancy more dangerous than an ampullary one?
cards.a: It implants in the part of the tube inside the uterine muscle, which is thicker and more vascular, so it ruptures later (around 12-16 weeks) and causes much heavier, life-threatening bleeding when it does.

cards.q: A woman has painless vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy and a barrel-shaped cervix with the external os dilated. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Cervical ectopic pregnancy. The embryo implants in the cervix, causing painless bleeding and a distended, hourglass-shaped cervix; it is dangerous because the cervix cannot contract to stop bleeding.

cards.q: After methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy, what follow-up is needed and what should the patient avoid?
cards.a: Follow beta-hCG until it falls to zero, usually with checks on days 4 and 7 and then weekly. Avoid folic acid supplements, NSAIDs, alcohol, and intercourse until beta-hCG is negative, because folic acid reverses methotrexate and NSAIDs and alcohol add toxicity.

cards.q: A woman has vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, a closed cervical os, and a live fetus on ultrasound. What type of miscarriage is this?
cards.a: Threatened abortion (threatened miscarriage). Bleeding with a closed os and a viable fetus means the pregnancy may still continue, so the next step is reassurance, pelvic rest, and follow-up ultrasound rather than evacuation.

cards.q: A woman has heavy vaginal bleeding, cramping, and a dilated cervical os with membranes bulging. What type of miscarriage is this?
cards.a: Inevitable abortion. Once the cervix is open and the pregnancy is being expelled, miscarriage cannot be prevented, so management is to support the process and evacuate retained tissue if bleeding is heavy.

cards.q: A woman has vaginal bleeding, an open os, and passage of some tissue but retained products on ultrasound. What type of miscarriage is this?
cards.a: Incomplete abortion. Some pregnancy tissue has passed but some remains in the uterus, which keeps bleeding going, so the uterus needs to be emptied (expectant, medical, or surgical management).

cards.q: A woman had vaginal bleeding and passed tissue, and now has a closed os, minimal bleeding, and an empty uterus on ultrasound. What type of miscarriage is this?
cards.a: Complete abortion. All pregnancy tissue has passed, the cervix has closed, and bleeding is settling, so no evacuation is needed; confirm with ultrasound and beta-hCG follow-up.

cards.q: A woman at 10 weeks has no bleeding or cramping, but ultrasound shows a fetus with no heartbeat. What is this called?
cards.a: Missed abortion (missed miscarriage). The fetus has died but the uterus has not expelled it, so there may be no symptoms at all; it is often found on routine ultrasound, and the pregnancy then needs medical or surgical evacuation.

cards.q: What are the three management options for early pregnancy loss, and when is surgery preferred?
cards.a: Expectant (wait for natural passage), medical (misoprostol, with or without mifepristone), and surgical (manual or electric vacuum aspiration). Surgery is preferred with heavy bleeding, haemodynamic instability, infection, or when the patient wants it done quickly and definitively.

cards.q: How does misoprostol work in the medical management of miscarriage?
cards.a: It is a prostaglandin E1 analogue that ripens and opens the cervix and causes uterine contractions, so the uterus expels the pregnancy tissue. It is the standard medical option for early pregnancy loss.

cards.q: A Rh-negative woman has a miscarriage at 9 weeks. What should she receive?
cards.a: Anti-D (Rh) immunoglobulin. Even a first-trimester miscarriage can expose an Rh-negative woman to Rh-positive fetal blood and sensitise her, which would endanger future pregnancies, so anti-D is given after any miscarriage.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of first-trimester miscarriage?
cards.a: Fetal chromosomal aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number, most often trisomy). Most early losses are due to a genetic error in the embryo that makes it nonviable, not anything the mother did.

cards.q: A woman has had two consecutive miscarriages. What workup is indicated for recurrent pregnancy loss?
cards.a: Test for antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2 glycoprotein), thyroid function, uterine anatomy (sonohysterography or hysteroscopy), and parental karyotypes. Recurrent loss is usually due to a treatable cause such as antiphospholipid syndrome or a uterine septum.

cards.q: Ultrasound shows a gestational sac but no embryo at 8 weeks. What is this called?
cards.a: Anembryonic pregnancy (blighted ovum). The sac develops but the embryo never forms or stops growing very early, usually due to a chromosomal abnormality, and it presents as a missed miscarriage.

cards.q: What organisms most commonly cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
cards.a: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. PID is an ascending infection from the cervix into the uterus, tubes, and ovaries, and these two sexually transmitted organisms are the usual culprits, often with polymicrobial involvement.

cards.q: A woman with PID has right upper quadrant pain. What syndrome is this and why does it happen?
cards.a: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, perihepatitis from PID. Infection spreads from the pelvis up the right paracolic gutter to the liver capsule, causing RUQ pain that mimics cholecystitis, with adhesions between the liver and abdominal wall.

cards.q: What are the minimum clinical criteria to diagnose PID?
cards.a: Pelvic pain plus one of: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. PID is a clinical diagnosis, so treat empirically when these are present rather than waiting for test results, because delay risks infertility.

cards.q: What is the outpatient antibiotic regimen for PID?
cards.a: Single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral doxycycline for 14 days plus metronidazole for 14 days. Ceftriaxone covers gonorrhoea, doxycycline covers chlamydia, and metronidazole covers anaerobes.

cards.q: When should a woman with PID be admitted to hospital instead of treated as an outpatient?
cards.a: If she has a tubo-ovarian abscess, is pregnant, is severely ill or vomiting and cannot take oral antibiotics, has failed outpatient treatment, or the diagnosis is uncertain. Admission allows IV antibiotics and close monitoring for abscess or sepsis.

cards.q: A woman with PID has fever, a tender pelvic mass, and leukocytosis. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Tubo-ovarian abscess (TOA). It is a walled-off collection of pus involving the tube and ovary, a complication of PID, and it can rupture into the abdomen causing peritonitis and sepsis.

cards.q: What is the treatment for a tubo-ovarian abscess?
cards.a: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (for example cefoxitin or cefotetan plus doxycycline, or clindamycin plus gentamicin) and hospital admission. Drainage (image-guided or surgical) is added if the abscess is large (over about 7-9 cm), ruptures, or does not improve after 48-72 hours of antibiotics.

cards.q: What are the long-term sequelae of PID?
cards.a: Tubal factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. PID scars and blocks the fallopian tubes, so early treatment matters more than anything else for preserving fertility.

cards.q: A woman with PID has an IUD in place. Should the IUD be removed?
cards.a: No, not routinely. The IUD is left in place and PID is treated with antibiotics; removal is considered only if there is no improvement after 48-72 hours. The highest PID risk is in the first 20 days after insertion, when insertion may have carried bacteria upward.

cards.q: Why is PID often diagnosed late, and what test confirms the causative organisms?
cards.a: Because chlamydia, the commonest cause, is often asymptomatic until the tubes are already damaged. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) of cervical or urine samples detects gonorrhoea and chlamydia, but treatment should start on clinical suspicion without waiting for results.

cards.q: What counselling should be given to a woman treated for PID?
cards.a: Her sexual partners from the last 60 days need testing and treatment, and she should abstain from intercourse until treatment is complete and partners are treated. Otherwise she will be reinfected, and repeated PID greatly increases the risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

cards.q: What does PALM stand for in the PALM-COEIN classification of abnormal uterine bleeding?
cards.a: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy and hyperplasia. PALM covers the structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding, which are diagnosed by imaging or histology.

cards.q: What does COEIN stand for in the PALM-COEIN classification of abnormal uterine bleeding?
cards.a: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, and Not yet classified. COEIN covers the non-structural causes of abnormal uterine bleeding.

cards.q: How is heavy menstrual bleeding defined?
cards.a: Menstrual blood loss over 80 mL per cycle, or bleeding heavy enough to interfere with a woman's physical, social, emotional, or work life. The practical definition is bleeding that affects her life, not just the measured volume.

cards.q: What is the first step in evaluating abnormal uterine bleeding?
cards.a: A pregnancy test, plus history, pelvic examination, and basic labs (CBC, TSH, prolactin, and coagulation studies if indicated). Pregnancy must always be excluded first in a reproductive-age woman with abnormal bleeding.

cards.q: A 14-year-old girl has heavy menstrual bleeding since her first period and easy bruising. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Von Willebrand disease, the commonest inherited bleeding disorder. Heavy bleeding from menarche in an adolescent, especially with bruising or nosebleeds, points to a coagulopathy rather than a hormonal cause.

cards.q: Which type of uterine leiomyoma (fibroid) is most likely to cause heavy menstrual bleeding?
cards.a: Submucosal leiomyoma. It grows just under the endometrium and distorts the uterine cavity, increasing the bleeding surface and preventing the uterus from contracting properly to stop bleeding.

cards.q: When is endometrial biopsy indicated in abnormal uterine bleeding?
cards.a: In women over 45, and in younger women with obesity, chronic anovulation, persistent bleeding, failed medical treatment, or abnormal ultrasound findings. The purpose is to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or cancer.

cards.q: What is the first-line medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding?
cards.a: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system (hormonal IUD). It releases progestin locally, thins the endometrium, and reduces bleeding more effectively than oral drugs, with few systemic side effects.

cards.q: How does tranexamic acid reduce menstrual blood loss?
cards.a: It is an antifibrinolytic: it blocks the breakdown of fibrin clots. Menstrual blood contains high levels of fibrinolytics, so tranexamic acid stabilises clots in the uterus and reduces bleeding without hormones.

cards.q: Why do NSAIDs help heavy menstrual bleeding?
cards.a: They inhibit prostaglandin production. Excess prostaglandins in the endometrium cause vasodilation and prevent platelet aggregation, so blocking them reduces blood flow and also relieves dysmenorrhoea.

cards.q: A woman presents with acute, severe uterine bleeding and haemodynamic instability. What is the immediate management?
cards.a: Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood, and give high-dose combined oral contraceptives or IV conjugated estrogen to stop the bleeding quickly. Acute heavy bleeding is managed first by stabilising the patient and using hormones to rapidly stabilise the endometrium.

cards.q: A 62-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding one year after menopause. What must be excluded first and how?
cards.a: Endometrial cancer. Any postmenopausal bleeding needs evaluation, starting with transvaginal ultrasound; an endometrial thickness over 4-5 mm, or persistent bleeding, needs endometrial sampling.

cards.q: A woman has sudden, severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting and a tender adnexal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Ovarian torsion. Sudden severe pain with nausea and vomiting is classic, because twisting of the ovary cuts off its blood supply and irritates the peritoneum; it is a surgical emergency.

cards.q: What is the most common cause of ovarian torsion in reproductive-age women?
cards.a: A benign ovarian mass or cyst, most often a mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) or a serous cystadenoma. The weight of the mass makes the ovary top-heavy so it twists on its ligament.

cards.q: A woman has intermittent, waxing and waning severe pelvic pain over several days. What does this suggest?
cards.a: Intermittent ovarian torsion. The ovary twists and untwists, causing pain that comes and goes, which is easy to miss; the ovary is still at risk of infarction, so it needs urgent evaluation.

cards.q: Doppler ultrasound of the ovary shows normal blood flow. Does this exclude ovarian torsion?
cards.a: No. Normal Doppler flow does not exclude torsion, because the ovary has a dual blood supply and flow can persist early on, or the ovary may have untwisted at the time of the scan. High clinical suspicion still needs surgical exploration.

cards.q: What is the next best step when ovarian torsion is strongly suspected?
cards.a: Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy. Torsion is a clinical diagnosis and time is ovary: delay for more imaging risks infarction, so do not wait for a confirmatory scan when suspicion is high.

cards.q: What is the surgical treatment for ovarian torsion, and why is the ovary usually conserved?
cards.a: Laparoscopic detorsion (untwisting) with cystectomy if a cyst is present, preserving the ovary. Even a dusky or blue-looking ovary often recovers after detorsion, so oophorectomy is reserved for a clearly necrotic ovary, especially in young women.

cards.q: A pregnant woman at 14 weeks has sudden severe pelvic pain and a 7 cm ovarian cyst. What is the management if torsion is suspected?
cards.a: Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion. Torsion in pregnancy is still a surgical emergency; laparoscopy is safe in pregnancy, and delay risks losing the ovary and the pregnancy.

cards.q: What factors increase the risk of ovarian torsion?
cards.a: An ovarian mass larger than 5 cm, pregnancy, and ovulation induction (which enlarges the ovaries). All make the ovary heavier and more mobile, so it is more likely to twist on its pedicle.

cards.q: What is the differential diagnosis of sudden severe pelvic pain in a young woman?
cards.a: Ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, ruptured ovarian cyst, PID or tubo-ovarian abscess, appendicitis, urinary tract infection or kidney stone, and severe dysmenorrhoea. A pregnancy test, ultrasound, and examination narrow this down, and torsion and ruptured ectopic are the cannot-miss emergencies.

cards.q: What is a complete hydatidiform mole?
cards.a: A molar pregnancy with no fetus, made of grape-like vesicles, with a diploid karyotype (usually 46,XX) that is entirely paternal in origin. An empty egg is fertilised by a sperm that duplicates, so there is no maternal DNA and no embryo.

cards.q: What is a partial hydatidiform mole?
cards.a: A molar pregnancy with some fetal tissue, with a triploid karyotype (69,XXX or 69,XXY) from two sperm fertilising one egg. Unlike a complete mole, a fetus may be present but it is abnormal and nonviable.

cards.q: A woman at 12 weeks has a uterus much larger than dates, severe hyperemesis, and a very high beta-hCG. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Complete hydatidiform mole. The molar tissue makes huge amounts of hCG, which overstimulates the uterus and causes severe nausea and vomiting, uterine enlargement, and sometimes early preeclampsia.

cards.q: What is the most common karyotype of a complete hydatidiform mole?
cards.a: 46,XX, diploid and entirely paternal. It arises when an empty ovum is fertilised by a single sperm that duplicates its chromosomes, so all the DNA comes from the father.

cards.q: What is the treatment for a hydatidiform mole?
cards.a: Suction curettage to evacuate the uterus. Oxytocin should not be given before evacuation because it can push molar tissue into the circulation; the uterus is emptied surgically and the tissue is sent for histology.

cards.q: After evacuation of a molar pregnancy, what follow-up is required and why must pregnancy be avoided?
cards.a: Weekly beta-hCG until negative three times, then monthly for 6 months, and reliable contraception for 6-12 months. Rising or plateauing hCG means persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, and a new pregnancy would raise hCG and hide that warning sign.

cards.q: Beta-hCG plateaus or rises after evacuation of a molar pregnancy. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (persistent molar disease). It means molar tissue is still growing, usually an invasive mole or choriocarcinoma, and it needs chemotherapy, not another curettage.

cards.q: What is choriocarcinoma and where does it commonly spread?
cards.a: A highly malignant tumour of trophoblast that follows a molar pregnancy, abortion, or normal pregnancy. It is very vascular and spreads early through blood to the lungs, vagina, and brain, and it makes extremely high amounts of beta-hCG.

cards.q: What is the treatment and prognosis of choriocarcinoma?
cards.a: Chemotherapy (methotrexate for low-risk disease, multi-agent EMA-CO for high-risk disease). Choriocarcinoma is highly chemosensitive and usually curable even with metastases, which is why beta-hCG follow-up after any molar pregnancy is so important.

cards.q: A woman with a molar pregnancy has bilateral large ovarian cysts. What are these and what happens to them?
cards.a: Theca lutein cysts, caused by very high hCG overstimulating the ovaries. They are benign and resolve on their own after the mole is evacuated and hCG falls, so they do not need surgery.

cards.q: What is the first step in evaluating vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy?
cards.a: Check vital signs, take a history, do a pregnancy test with quantitative beta-hCG, and arrange transvaginal ultrasound. The priorities are to exclude haemodynamic instability and ectopic pregnancy, which are the life-threatening causes.

cards.q: A woman at 8 weeks has vaginal bleeding, a viable fetus, and a crescent-shaped collection beside the sac on ultrasound. What is this?
cards.a: Subchorionic haematoma. Blood collects between the chorion and the uterine wall; most small ones resolve and the pregnancy continues, but larger ones increase the risk of miscarriage.

cards.q: A woman has light spotting 7 days after ovulation with a barely positive pregnancy test. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a: Implantation bleeding. Light spotting occurs when the embryo implants into the endometrium, about 6-12 days after conception; it is brief and light, unlike the heavier bleeding of miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy.

cards.q: A woman of reproductive age presents with acute pelvic pain. What is the most important first test?
cards.a: A urine pregnancy test. It immediately divides the differential: a positive test makes ectopic pregnancy the priority, while a negative test points toward torsion, ruptured cyst, PID, or appendicitis.

cards.q: A woman has a positive pregnancy test, pelvic pain, and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas on ultrasound. What should you assume?
cards.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Free fluid in a pregnant woman with pain is blood until shown to be something else, and this is a surgical emergency.

cards.q: Ultrasound in early pregnancy shows a fluid collection in the uterus but no yolk sac or fetal pole. What is this called?
cards.a: A pseudogestational sac. It is fluid or blood in the endometrial cavity that mimics a true gestational sac in an ectopic pregnancy, whereas a true sac is eccentrically placed with a double decidual sign.

cards.q: A woman at 7 weeks has mild unilateral pelvic pain and a 3 cm simple cyst on ultrasound. What is the likely cause and its course?
cards.a: A corpus luteum cyst of pregnancy. It forms after ovulation and makes progesterone to support the early pregnancy, usually causes only mild pain, and resolves on its own by the second trimester.

cards.q: A woman has a positive pregnancy test but no intrauterine or ectopic pregnancy is seen on ultrasound. What is this called and what is the next step?
cards.a: A pregnancy of unknown location. Repeat quantitative beta-hCG in 48 hours and repeat ultrasound; a rising hCG with no visible pregnancy needs close follow-up because ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded.

cards.q: What are the causes of acute pelvic pain that must not be missed?
cards.a: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured ovarian cyst with haemoperitoneum, and tubo-ovarian abscess. All four can cause peritonitis, sepsis, or death, so they are the first things to exclude in a woman with sudden severe pelvic pain.

cards.q: A woman has sudden severe pelvic pain in the middle of her menstrual cycle with a small amount of free fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
cards.a: Ruptured functional ovarian cyst (ruptured follicular or corpus luteum cyst). Mid-cycle rupture causes sudden pain and a small amount of bleeding into the abdomen, and it usually settles on its own with observation and pain relief.

cards.q: Why does a ruptured corpus luteum cyst bleed more than a ruptured follicular cyst?
cards.a: Because the corpus luteum is highly vascular, with a rich blood supply to support progesterone production. Rupture can therefore cause significant haemoperitoneum, especially in a woman on anticoagulants.

cards.q: A woman with a ruptured ovarian cyst is hypotensive with a falling haemoglobin. What is the management?
cards.a: Resuscitation with IV fluids and blood and urgent surgery (laparoscopy or laparotomy) to control the bleeding. A haemodynamically unstable patient with haemoperitoneum needs operative control of bleeding, not observation.

cards.q: A haemodynamically stable woman has a ruptured ovarian cyst with mild pain and a small amount of free fluid. What is the management?
cards.a: Observation, analgesia, and monitoring. Most ruptured functional cysts stop bleeding on their own, so stable patients are watched with repeat examination and haemoglobin rather than rushed to surgery.

cards.q: Ultrasound shows an ovarian cyst with a fine, lace-like (reticular) internal pattern. What is this?
cards.a: A haemorrhagic ovarian cyst. Blood inside the cyst forms fibrin strands that look like lace or a spiderweb on ultrasound; it usually resolves over a few weeks.

cards.q: A woman has sudden severe pelvic pain and a negative pregnancy test. How does this change the differential?
cards.a: It makes ectopic pregnancy very unlikely and points to a ruptured ovarian cyst, ovarian torsion, PID, or appendicitis. A negative pregnancy test is the single most useful test for narrowing acute pelvic pain.

cards.q: A woman has brief, sharp unilateral pelvic pain in the middle of her cycle that resolves in hours. What is this called?
cards.a: Mittelschmerz, ovulation pain. It is caused by the follicle rupturing and a small amount of fluid irritating the peritoneum, and it lasts hours to a day, unlike torsion or rupture which persist and worsen.

cards.q: A woman with known endometriosis has sudden severe pelvic pain and a collapsed ovarian cyst on ultrasound. What happened?
cards.a: Rupture of an endometrioma (chocolate cyst). Endometriomas contain old blood, and rupture spills irritating contents into the abdomen causing severe pain and peritonitis, often needing surgery.

cards.q: A woman has fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, and uterine tenderness one week after a miscarriage. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Septic abortion. Infection of retained products of conception after miscarriage or induced abortion causes fever, offensive discharge, and a tender uterus, and it can progress rapidly to sepsis.

cards.q: What organisms most commonly cause septic abortion, and which one can cause haemolysis?
cards.a: Escherichia coli, group B streptococcus, and anaerobes, often polymicrobial. Clostridium perfringens can cause severe haemolysis and jaundice, which is a classic clue to a clostridial infection after abortion.

cards.q: What is the next best step in a woman with septic abortion?
cards.a: Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgently evacuate the uterus. Antibiotics alone cannot clear infected retained tissue, so evacuation must not be delayed while waiting for antibiotics to work.

cards.q: What are the complications of septic abortion?
cards.a: Sepsis and septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), acute renal failure, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Septic abortion is a leading cause of maternal death worldwide, so it needs immediate antibiotics and evacuation.

cards.q: What is the main risk factor for septic abortion?
cards.a: Unsafe or illegal abortion, and retained products of conception after any abortion or miscarriage. Retained tissue is an ideal medium for bacterial growth, which is why evacuation and follow-up matter.

cards.q: What is the difference between a Bartholin cyst and a Bartholin abscess?
cards.a: A Bartholin cyst is a painless, non-tender swelling from a blocked duct, while an abscess is painful, tender, red, and hot from infection of the cyst. The Bartholin glands sit at 4 and 8 o'clock at the vaginal opening and lubricate the vestibule.

cards.q: What organisms cause a Bartholin abscess?
cards.a: Usually polymicrobial, most often Escherichia coli and other gut and vaginal flora, sometimes with gonorrhoea or chlamydia. Testing for sexually transmitted infections is part of the workup.

cards.q: What is the treatment for a Bartholin abscess?
cards.a: Incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter. The catheter keeps the tract open so a new duct forms and the abscess does not recur; simple drainage alone has a high recurrence rate.

cards.q: A Bartholin abscess keeps recurring despite drainage. What is the definitive treatment?
cards.a: Marsupialisation. The cyst wall is stitched open to the skin to create a permanent drainage opening, which is used for recurrent cysts or abscesses that fail Word catheter treatment.

cards.q: A woman has fever, hypotension, a diffuse sunburn-like rash, and vomiting after using a tampon. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS). The classic features are high fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma, mucosal hyperaemia, and multiorgan involvement, with peeling of the palms and soles 1-2 weeks later.

cards.q: What causes toxic shock syndrome and how does the toxin work?
cards.a: Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) from Staphylococcus aureus, or a similar toxin from Streptococcus pyogenes. It is a superantigen that activates a huge number of T cells at once, causing a massive cytokine release and shock.

cards.q: What is the immediate management of toxic shock syndrome?
cards.a: Remove the source (for example the tampon), give aggressive IV fluids, admit to intensive care, and start IV antibiotics such as clindamycin plus vancomycin or nafcillin. Clindamycin is added because it switches off toxin production.

cards.q: A woman recovering from toxic shock syndrome develops peeling of the palms and soles two weeks later. What is this?
cards.a: Desquamation, the classic late feature of toxic shock syndrome. Peeling of the palms and soles 1-2 weeks after the illness confirms the diagnosis retrospectively.

cards.q: What is the first priority when a woman presents after a sexual assault?
cards.a: Her safety, consent, and medical stabilisation, then a trauma-informed history and examination. Care is given only with her consent at each step, and she is offered a forensic examination, emergency contraception, STI prophylaxis, and HIV post-exposure prophylaxis.

cards.q: Within what time window should a forensic examination be offered after a sexual assault?
cards.a: Within 72-120 hours, depending on local protocol. Evidence collection is most useful early, but care, emergency contraception, and prophylaxis should never be refused just because the window has passed.

cards.q: What emergency contraception is offered after a sexual assault and when?
cards.a: Emergency contraception within 120 hours of the assault, most effectively levonorgestrel within 72 hours, or a copper IUD within 5 days. It prevents pregnancy from the assault, so it should be offered promptly.

cards.q: What STI prophylaxis is given after a sexual assault?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone (single intramuscular dose) plus azithromycin (single oral dose) plus metronidazole or doxycycline. This covers gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis in one empiric regimen.

cards.q: When is HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) indicated after a sexual assault?
