cards.a: When the assailant is known to be HIV-positive or the risk is high, started within 72 hours and taken for 28 days. PEP is most effective the earlier it starts, so it should be offered urgently, not after waiting for test results.

cards.q: What other preventive care is offered after a sexual assault?
cards.a: Hepatitis B vaccination if not immune, tetanus vaccination if indicated, and baseline and follow-up testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis. She is also offered counselling, safety planning, and referral to support services, with documentation and chain of custody for any forensic samples.

cards.q: What is ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) and what triggers it?
cards.a: A complication of ovulation induction or IVF, triggered by human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). hCG makes the ovaries enlarge and blood vessels leak, so fluid shifts out of the circulation into the abdomen and chest.

cards.q: A woman after IVF has abdominal distension, weight gain, nausea, and dyspnoea. What is the diagnosis?
cards.a: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS). Enlarged ovaries and third-spacing of fluid cause abdominal distension, rapid weight gain, nausea, and breathlessness from ascites or pleural effusion.

cards.q: What laboratory findings are seen in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?
cards.a: Haemoconcentration (high haematocrit), leukocytosis, electrolyte disturbance, and low albumin. Fluid leaking out of the vessels concentrates the blood, which is why the haematocrit rises.

cards.q: What are the severe complications of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?
cards.a: Massive ascites, pleural effusion, oliguria and renal failure, and thromboembolism. The combination of haemoconcentration and immobility makes clots a major risk, so thromboprophylaxis is important.

cards.q: What is the management of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?
cards.a: Supportive care: IV fluids, monitoring of weight, urine output and haematocrit, and thromboprophylaxis. Paracentesis is reserved for severe respiratory compromise, and hCG should be avoided because it worsens the syndrome.

cards.q: A woman has bleeding after intercourse. What are the common causes?
cards.a: Cervical ectropion, cervicitis from chlamydia or gonorrhoea, a cervical polyp, and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer. Post-coital bleeding always needs a speculum examination and cervical screening, because it can be the first sign of cervical cancer.

cards.q: What is the first step in evaluating post-coital bleeding?
cards.a: Speculum examination, cervical screening (Pap smear and HPV testing), and testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. Examination looks for a visible lesion or ectropion, and screening excludes precancer and infection.

cards.q: A young woman on oral contraceptives has post-coital bleeding and a red, velvety area around the cervical os. What is this?
cards.a: Cervical ectropion (cervical erosion). Glandular epithelium from inside the canal extends onto the ectocervix; it is fragile and bleeds on contact, and it is common in adolescents, pregnancy, and oral contraceptive users.

cards.q: A woman has post-coital bleeding and a visible friable lesion on the cervix. What is the next step?
cards.a: Refer for colposcopy and biopsy. A visible cervical lesion must never just be reassured away, because it may be cervical cancer or high-grade dysplasia.

cards.q: A postmenopausal woman has bleeding after intercourse. What must be excluded?
cards.a: Cervical or endometrial malignancy, and also atrophic vaginitis. Postmenopausal bleeding of any kind, including after intercourse, needs examination, cervical screening, and endometrial assessment.

cards.q: After methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy, the beta-hCG rises on day 4. Is this treatment failure?
cards.a: No, a rise on day 4 is expected and does not mean failure. Methotrexate takes time to kill the trophoblast, so the key check is a fall of at least 15% between day 4 and day 7; if it does not fall enough, a second dose is given.

cards.q: A woman with recurrent miscarriage is found to have antiphospholipid syndrome. What treatment is given in her next pregnancy?
cards.a: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin (such as low-molecular-weight heparin) throughout pregnancy. Antiphospholipid antibodies cause clotting in the placental vessels, and this combination prevents those clots and improves the chance of a live birth.

cards.q: A woman with a tubo-ovarian abscess suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, rigidity, and hypotension. What happened and what is the next step?
cards.a: The abscess has ruptured, spilling pus into the abdomen and causing peritonitis and sepsis. This needs resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and emergency surgery to wash out the abdomen and remove the source.

cards.q: A perimenopausal woman has irregular heavy bleeding with long gaps between periods. What is the mechanism?
cards.a: Anovulatory bleeding from unopposed estrogen. Without ovulation there is no progesterone to stabilise the endometrium, so it grows under estrogen alone and sheds irregularly and heavily, which over time raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia.

cards.q: Ultrasound shows no ovarian mass in a woman with sudden severe pelvic pain and vomiting. Can ovarian torsion be excluded?
cards.a: No. Torsion can occur in a normal ovary, especially in children and adolescents, and an ovary that has untwisted may look normal on ultrasound. Persistent severe pain with vomiting still needs urgent surgical evaluation.

cards.q: Which type of molar pregnancy carries a higher risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, complete or partial?
cards.a: Complete mole. Complete moles are much more likely to develop persistent trophoblastic disease than partial moles, which is why beta-hCG surveillance is especially important after a complete mole.

cards.q: How can ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome be prevented in a woman undergoing IVF?
cards.a: By using a GnRH agonist trigger instead of hCG to mature the eggs, and by freezing all embryos rather than transferring fresh. OHSS is driven by hCG, so avoiding an hCG trigger greatly reduces the risk.

cards.q: How do combined oral contraceptives (COCs) prevent pregnancy?
cards.a: They mainly suppress ovulation by inhibiting gonadotropin release from the pituitary, so no egg is released. The progestin also thickens cervical mucus to block sperm and thins the endometrium, making implantation unlikely. This is why they work only if taken consistently.

cards.q: What is the typical-use failure rate of COCs compared with perfect use?
cards.a: With perfect use about 0.3 in 100 women become pregnant in a year, but with typical use about 7 in 100 do, because missed or late pills are common. This gap is why counselling about adherence matters and why long-acting methods are often preferred.

cards.q: What are the main non-contraceptive benefits of COCs?
cards.a: They reduce menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhea, regulate irregular cycles, improve acne and hirsutism, and lower the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer and benign ovarian cysts. These benefits come from ovulation suppression and the steady hormone levels.

cards.q: A woman with a history of deep vein thrombosis wants a COC. What do you do?
cards.a: Do not prescribe a COC. Estrogen increases clotting factors and the risk of venous thromboembolism, so a prior VTE is a contraindication (MEC category 4). Offer a progestin-only or non-hormonal method such as a copper IUD instead.

cards.q: A 38-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes a day asks for a COC. What is the concern?
cards.a: Do not prescribe a COC. Smoking plus age 35 or older plus estrogen markedly raises the risk of arterial thrombosis, including myocardial infarction and stroke. Offer a progestin-only method or an IUD instead.

cards.q: Why are COCs contraindicated in migraine with aura?
cards.a: Migraine with aura already raises the risk of ischemic stroke, and estrogen adds further stroke risk, so the combination is unsafe (MEC category 4). A progestin-only method or a copper IUD is safer because it avoids estrogen.

cards.q: What should be checked before starting a COC?
cards.a: Take a focused history for contraindications such as VTE, stroke, migraine with aura, smoking over age 35, and breast cancer, and measure blood pressure. Estrogen can raise blood pressure, so an elevated reading must be addressed before starting.

cards.q: Why are COCs contraindicated in current breast cancer?
cards.a: Most breast cancers are hormone-sensitive, so estrogen and progestin could stimulate tumour growth. Hormonal contraception is avoided during active breast cancer; a copper IUD is the preferred reversible option.

cards.q: When can a woman start a COC, and when is backup contraception needed?
cards.a: She can start any day if pregnancy is reasonably excluded (quick start). If she starts within the first 5 days of her period no backup is needed; otherwise she needs condoms or abstinence for the first 7 days while ovulation suppression takes effect.

cards.q: Why do COCs help acne and hirsutism?
cards.a: Estrogen raises sex hormone-binding globulin, which binds free testosterone, and the progestin suppresses ovarian androgen production. Less free androgen means less stimulation of sebaceous glands and hair follicles.

cards.q: How do COCs affect the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer?
cards.a: They reduce the risk of both cancers, and the protection grows with longer use and persists for years after stopping. Suppressing ovulation protects the ovary, and the progestin opposes estrogen-driven growth of the endometrium.

cards.q: A woman has light spotting during her first 2 months on a COC. What do you tell her?
cards.a: Reassure her that breakthrough bleeding is common in the first 3 months as the endometrium adjusts, and it usually settles. Check adherence and smoking, and only investigate further if bleeding persists beyond 3 months or is heavy.

cards.q: A woman is less than 24 hours late taking one active COC pill. What should she do?
cards.a: Take the missed pill as soon as she remembers and continue the pack as normal, even if that means taking two pills in one day. No backup contraception is needed because ovulation suppression is not lost after a single short delay.

cards.q: A woman misses one active pill in week 1 of her pack and had sex in the previous 5 days. What is the next step?
cards.a: Take the missed pill now, use condoms for 7 days, and consider emergency contraception. Missing a pill in week 1 is the riskiest because the hormone-free interval is effectively lengthened and ovulation may occur.

cards.q: A woman misses one active pill in week 2 of her pack. What should she do?
cards.a: Take the missed pill as soon as she remembers and continue the pack; no backup contraception is needed if she took the previous 7 pills correctly. By week 2 ovulation is already suppressed, so a single missed pill is low risk.

cards.q: A woman misses pills in week 3 of her pack. What should she do?
cards.a: Take the missed pill, finish the active pills, and skip the hormone-free interval by starting the next pack immediately. This avoids lengthening the pill-free gap, which is when ovulation is most likely to escape suppression.

cards.q: A woman misses two or more active COC pills in a row. What is the advice?
cards.a: Take the most recent missed pill now, discard the others, continue the pack, and use condoms or abstain for 7 days. Consider emergency contraception if she had unprotected sex in the last 5 days, because ovulation suppression may have been lost.

cards.q: When is emergency contraception needed after missed COC pills?
cards.a: Consider it if she missed pills in week 1 and had unprotected sex in the last 5 days, or missed two or more pills and had sex since the last correctly taken pill. The risk is ovulation occurring before suppression is re-established.

cards.q: A woman vomits within 2 hours of taking her COC pill. What should she do?
cards.a: Treat it as a missed pill: take another active pill as soon as possible, because the pill may not have been absorbed. If vomiting continues, use backup contraception and consider switching to a non-oral method.

cards.q: When can a COC be started after a first-trimester abortion?
cards.a: Immediately, on the same day if possible. Ovulation can return within 2 weeks of an abortion, so starting right away prevents a new pregnancy, and there is no increased VTE risk in this setting.

cards.q: Why does rifampicin reduce COC effectiveness?
cards.a: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of liver enzymes that metabolise estrogen and progestin, so hormone levels fall and ovulation can occur. Women on rifampicin should use a non-hormonal method such as a copper IUD, not a COC.

cards.q: A woman with epilepsy on carbamazepine wants a COC. What is the problem?
cards.a: Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes that speed up breakdown of estrogen and progestin, lowering their levels and risking contraceptive failure. It also lowers seizure control indirectly, so a copper IUD or levonorgestrel IUD is preferred.

cards.q: Why is efavirenz a problem for women using hormonal contraception?
cards.a: Efavirenz induces liver enzymes that reduce levels of estrogen, progestin and etonogestrel, so pills and implants can fail. An IUD is preferred because its action is mainly local and is not affected by liver enzyme induction.

cards.q: A woman on a COC is prescribed amoxicillin for a urinary infection. Does she need backup contraception?
cards.a: No. Ordinary antibiotics such as amoxicillin, doxycycline and nitrofurantoin do not reduce COC effectiveness. Only rifampicin and related rifamycins are the important exception, so she can continue her pills as normal.

cards.q: A woman with epilepsy takes lamotrigine and starts a COC. What interaction must you warn about?
cards.a: Estrogen increases the clearance of lamotrigine, so lamotrigine levels can fall by about half and seizures may break through. Her neurologist should monitor levels and adjust the dose; a non-estrogen method avoids this problem.

cards.q: Why can St John's wort reduce COC effectiveness?
cards.a: St John's wort induces liver enzymes that increase metabolism of estrogen and progestin, lowering hormone levels and risking ovulation. Women using it should choose a method not affected by enzyme induction, such as a copper IUD.

cards.q: How do progestin-only pills (POPs) prevent pregnancy?
cards.a: They mainly thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and about half of cycles also suppress ovulation. Because mucus thickening is short-lived, timing matters much more than with COCs.

cards.q: What is the timing window for a traditional progestin-only pill?
cards.a: It must be taken within 3 hours of the same time each day; more than 3 hours late counts as a missed pill. The desogestrel POP has a 12-hour window because it reliably suppresses ovulation, but the 3-hour rule is the classic exam point.

cards.q: A woman is 5 hours late taking her traditional POP. What should she do?
cards.a: Take the pill as soon as she remembers, continue the pack, and use condoms or abstain for 48 hours. The cervical mucus effect wears off quickly, so sperm could pass through before protection returns.

cards.q: Why are POPs safe during breastfeeding?
cards.a: They contain no estrogen, so they do not reduce milk supply, and only tiny amounts of progestin pass into breast milk with no known harm to the infant. This makes them a first-line choice for breastfeeding women who want a pill.

cards.q: A woman becomes pregnant while taking a POP. Why is ectopic pregnancy relatively more likely?
cards.a: POPs do not always suppress ovulation, but progestin slows tubal motility, so if fertilisation does occur the embryo is more likely to implant in the tube. Any pregnant POP user with pain or bleeding needs urgent assessment for ectopic pregnancy.

cards.q: What is the commonest side effect of POPs?
cards.a: Irregular bleeding, including frequent spotting, irregular periods or amenorrhea. It is caused by the progestin effect on the endometrium and is the main reason women stop POPs, though it often improves with time.

cards.q: Why are POPs an option when COCs are contraindicated?
cards.a: POPs contain no estrogen, so they do not carry the estrogen-related risks of venous thromboembolism, stroke or myocardial infarction. They can be used by smokers over 35, women with migraine with aura, and women with a history of VTE.

cards.q: A woman with migraine with aura needs contraception. Why is a POP acceptable but a COC is not?
cards.a: Migraine with aura raises stroke risk and estrogen adds to it, but progestin alone does not increase stroke risk. A POP therefore gives effective contraception without the estrogen-related vascular risk.

cards.q: How does depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) work and how often is it given?
cards.a: It is a progestin injection given intramuscularly every 13 weeks that suppresses ovulation, thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium. The long interval makes it useful for women who struggle with daily pills.

cards.q: How effective is DMPA with typical use?
cards.a: About 4 in 100 women become pregnant in the first year with typical use, mainly because injections are given late. With perfect on-time use the failure rate is under 1 in 100, so a reminder system matters.

cards.q: What should a woman be counselled about DMPA and bone density?
cards.a: DMPA lowers estrogen levels, which can reduce bone mineral density, especially in the first 2 years, but the loss is largely reversible after stopping. It is not a reason to withhold DMPA from most women, including adolescents, but calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise should be encouraged.

cards.q: What is the commonest reason women stop DMPA?
cards.a: Weight gain and irregular bleeding. Average weight gain is a few kilograms in the first year, and irregular bleeding or amenorrhea is very common early on. Counselling about these effects before starting improves continuation.

cards.q: How long can fertility be delayed after stopping DMPA?
cards.a: Return to fertility can take up to 10 months after the last injection, with a median delay of about 10 months, because the depot releases progestin slowly. Women who want to conceive soon should choose a method with immediate return of fertility instead.

cards.q: Why is DMPA safe during breastfeeding?
cards.a: It contains no estrogen, so it does not reduce milk supply, and only small amounts of progestin enter breast milk without known harm to the infant. It can be started in the immediate postpartum period.

cards.q: A woman on DMPA has no periods at all after a year. What do you tell her?
cards.a: Reassure her that amenorrhea is expected and common with DMPA, occurring in about half of users by one year, because the endometrium becomes thin and atrophic. It is not harmful and does not mean she is pregnant or infertile.

cards.q: A woman on DMPA has bothersome irregular bleeding in the first 3 months. How do you manage it?
cards.a: Reassure her that it is common and often settles, and exclude pregnancy and infection. A short course of an NSAID or a short course of estrogen can help if bleeding persists, but changing method is reasonable if it is unacceptable to her.

cards.q: Why is DMPA contraindicated in current breast cancer?
cards.a: DMPA is a progestin and most breast cancers are hormone-sensitive, so it could stimulate tumour growth. A non-hormonal method such as a copper IUD is preferred until the cancer is treated.

cards.q: Why is DMPA sometimes preferred in women with sickle cell disease?
cards.a: DMPA reduces menstrual blood loss and the frequency of sickle cell crises, and it avoids estrogen, which would add thrombotic risk. It is therefore a good choice for women with sickle cell disease who need contraception.

cards.q: How does the etonogestrel implant work and how long does it last?
cards.a: A single rod under the skin of the upper arm releases etonogestrel continuously for 3 years, suppressing ovulation and thickening cervical mucus. It is one of the most effective reversible methods because it does not depend on the user remembering anything.

cards.q: How effective is the contraceptive implant?
cards.a: Fewer than 1 in 1000 women become pregnant in a year, making it the most effective reversible method along with IUDs. Effectiveness does not depend on daily adherence, which is why it is recommended first-line for adolescents.

cards.q: What is the commonest side effect of the etonogestrel implant?
cards.a: Unpredictable bleeding, including frequent or prolonged spotting, irregular bleeding or amenorrhea. Counselling about this before insertion is the best way to prevent early removal.

cards.q: When can the implant be inserted, and when is backup needed?
cards.a: It can be inserted any day if pregnancy is excluded. If inserted within the first 5 days of the period no backup is needed; otherwise condoms are needed for 7 days while ovulation suppression takes effect.

cards.q: Why can enzyme-inducing drugs reduce implant effectiveness?
cards.a: Drugs such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and rifampicin induce liver enzymes that increase breakdown of etonogestrel, so blood levels fall and ovulation can occur. Women on these drugs should use an IUD instead.

cards.q: How quickly does fertility return after implant removal?
cards.a: Immediately, usually within days to weeks, because there is no depot effect once the rod is out. This makes the implant a good choice for women who may want to conceive soon after stopping.

cards.q: Why is the implant contraindicated in current breast cancer?
cards.a: It releases progestin continuously, and hormone-sensitive breast cancer could be stimulated by it. A copper IUD is the preferred reversible method in this situation.

cards.q: Does obesity reduce the effectiveness of the contraceptive implant?
cards.a: No, the implant remains highly effective in women with obesity, and its failure rate stays very low. It is therefore a good first-line option for women with a high BMI who want highly effective contraception.

cards.q: How does the copper IUD prevent pregnancy?
cards.a: Copper ions are toxic to sperm and ova and create a local inflammatory reaction in the uterus that prevents fertilisation and implantation. It contains no hormones, so it does not suppress ovulation.

cards.q: How long does the copper IUD last, and how effective is it?
cards.a: It lasts up to 10 years and fewer than 1 in 100 women become pregnant in a year. It is one of the most effective reversible methods and is fully reversible on removal.

cards.q: What is the main menstrual side effect of the copper IUD?
cards.a: Heavier, longer and more painful periods, especially in the first few months. This is the commonest reason for removal, so women with already heavy periods are usually offered a levonorgestrel IUD instead.

cards.q: Why is the copper IUD the most effective form of emergency contraception?
cards.a: It can be inserted up to 5 days after unprotected sex, or up to 5 days after the earliest estimated ovulation, and it prevents fertilisation and implantation with a failure rate under 1 in 1000. It also provides ongoing contraception for years afterwards.

cards.q: Can a nulliparous woman or an adolescent use an IUD?
cards.a: Yes. Nulliparity and adolescence are not contraindications, and IUDs are recommended first-line for adolescents because they are highly effective and do not depend on adherence. Insertion may be slightly more uncomfortable but is safe.

cards.q: When is the risk of pelvic infection highest after IUD insertion?
cards.a: In the first 3 weeks after insertion, mainly from bacteria introduced during the procedure or from a pre-existing sexually transmitted infection. Screening for chlamydia and gonorrhoea before insertion and using sterile technique reduce this risk.

cards.q: Why is a copper IUD avoided in Wilson disease or copper allergy?
cards.a: Wilson disease causes copper accumulation in the body, and a copper IUD releases copper locally, so it could theoretically worsen copper overload. A levonorgestrel IUD or another method is used instead.

cards.q: A woman becomes pregnant with a copper IUD in place. Why is ectopic pregnancy more likely?
cards.a: The IUD prevents intrauterine pregnancy very effectively, but if fertilisation does occur, the chance that the pregnancy is ectopic is higher than in the general population. Any pregnant IUD user with pain or bleeding needs urgent ultrasound to exclude ectopic pregnancy.

cards.q: How does the levonorgestrel IUD prevent pregnancy?
cards.a: It releases levonorgestrel locally into the uterus, thickening cervical mucus, thinning the endometrium and partly suppressing ovulation. Because the hormone acts mainly locally, systemic levels are low.

cards.q: How long do the different levonorgestrel IUDs last?
cards.a: The 52 mg devices last up to 8 years, the 19.5 mg device up to 5 years, and the 13.5 mg device up to 3 years. All are highly effective, with fewer than 1 in 100 pregnancies per year.

cards.q: Why is the levonorgestrel IUD used to treat heavy menstrual bleeding?
cards.a: It thins the endometrium and reduces menstrual blood loss by over 90 percent in many women, often causing amenorrhea. It is first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding when contraception is also wanted and there is no structural cause needing surgery.

cards.q: A woman with a levonorgestrel IUD has no periods after a year. What do you tell her?
cards.a: Reassure her that amenorrhea is common and expected because the endometrium becomes very thin. It is not harmful, does not mean she is menopausal, and fertility returns quickly after removal.

cards.q: When can a levonorgestrel IUD be inserted after delivery?
cards.a: It can be inserted immediately after delivery of the placenta, within 48 hours, or delayed until at least 4 weeks postpartum. Insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks carries a higher expulsion risk, so that window is usually avoided.

cards.q: Why is the expulsion rate higher when an IUD is inserted immediately postpartum?
cards.a: The uterus is enlarged and the cervix is dilated, so the device is more likely to be expelled as the uterus involutes. Immediate insertion is still offered because many women do not return for a later visit, but they should be counselled about the higher expulsion risk.

cards.q: When should an IUD not be inserted?
cards.a: Do not insert an IUD with current pelvic inflammatory disease, purulent cervicitis, known chlamydia or gonorrhoea, or current pregnancy. A levonorgestrel IUD is also avoided in current breast cancer. Treat the infection first, then insert.

cards.q: A woman cannot feel her IUD strings. What is the next step?
cards.a: Exclude pregnancy, then examine the cervix and arrange an ultrasound to locate the device. The strings may have retracted into the cervix, the device may have been expelled, or rarely it may have perforated the uterus, so imaging is needed before assuming it is still in place.

cards.q: Why is the risk of uterine perforation higher when an IUD is inserted while breastfeeding?
cards.a: The postpartum uterus is soft and thin-walled with low estrogen, so the inserter can more easily pass through the uterine wall. Perforation is still rare, but insertion should be done carefully and the woman counselled to report severe pain.

cards.q: How does levonorgestrel emergency contraception work and when is it given?
cards.a: A single 1.5 mg dose taken as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours and up to 5 days after unprotected sex, delays or prevents ovulation. It is most effective the sooner it is taken and does not work once ovulation has already happened.

cards.q: Why does levonorgestrel emergency contraception become less effective with time?
cards.a: It works by delaying ovulation, so the longer the delay after sex, the more likely ovulation has already occurred or is about to occur. Taking it immediately gives the best chance of preventing fertilisation.

cards.q: How does ulipristal acetate emergency contraception differ from levonorgestrel?
cards.a: Ulipristal is a progesterone receptor modulator that can delay ovulation even after the luteinising hormone surge has begun, so it works up to 5 days after sex and is more effective than levonorgestrel, especially on days 3 to 5 and in women with a higher BMI.

cards.q: A woman takes ulipristal for emergency contraception and wants to restart her progestin pill. What must she wait for?
cards.a: She must wait 5 days before restarting any progestin-containing contraception, because progestin can reduce ulipristal's effect and ulipristal can reduce the progestin's effect. She should use condoms until her next period.

cards.q: Why is the copper IUD the best emergency contraception for a woman who presents 4 days after unprotected sex?
cards.a: It is effective up to 5 days after sex or ovulation regardless of timing, with a failure rate under 1 in 1000, far better than oral methods at this stage. It also gives her highly effective ongoing contraception for up to 10 years.

cards.q: Why is levonorgestrel emergency contraception less effective in women weighing over 75 kg?
cards.a: Higher body weight lowers the drug concentration, so ovulation may not be delayed. Ulipristal or a copper IUD is preferred in women with a higher BMI, and doubling the levonorgestrel dose is sometimes used if no other option is available.

cards.q: Does emergency contraception cause abortion?
cards.a: No. Levonorgestrel and ulipristal work by delaying or preventing ovulation, and the copper IUD prevents fertilisation. None of them disrupts an established pregnancy or harms an embryo if one is already implanted.

cards.q: A woman had unprotected sex 2 days ago and is already mid-cycle. Will levonorgestrel emergency contraception help?
cards.a: It may help only if ovulation has not yet occurred, because it works by delaying ovulation. If she has already ovulated, it will not prevent pregnancy, so a copper IUD is the better option at this stage.

cards.q: Does emergency contraception harm an existing pregnancy?
cards.a: No. If the woman is already pregnant, levonorgestrel and ulipristal do not cause miscarriage or birth defects. A pregnancy test should still be done, and the copper IUD must not be inserted if pregnancy is already established.

cards.q: Can emergency contraception be used more than once in the same cycle?
cards.a: Yes, it can be repeated if there is another episode of unprotected sex, but it is not a regular method because it is less effective than ongoing contraception and causes irregular bleeding. She should be offered a reliable ongoing method.

cards.q: A woman missed COC pills and had unprotected sex 3 days ago. What do you offer?
cards.a: Offer emergency contraception, preferably ulipristal or a copper IUD, and restart her COC with 7 days of backup contraception. The missed pills may have allowed ovulation, so emergency contraception is needed for the recent exposure.

cards.q: How effective is tubal ligation and is it reversible?
cards.a: It is over 99 percent effective, with about 5 in 1000 failures over 10 years, but it should be considered permanent. Reversal surgery is expensive, not always successful, and not guaranteed, so women must be certain they do not want more children.

cards.q: A woman becomes pregnant after tubal ligation. What complication must be excluded first?
cards.a: Ectopic pregnancy, because a large proportion of pregnancies after tubal ligation are ectopic. Any woman with a prior tubal ligation who presents with pain, bleeding or a positive pregnancy test needs urgent assessment.

cards.q: When can tubal ligation be performed in relation to delivery?
cards.a: It can be done immediately postpartum, usually within 48 hours, when the uterus is still enlarged and the tubes are easily reached, or as an interval procedure at least 6 weeks after delivery. Postpartum ligation avoids a second anaesthetic.

cards.q: Which women are most likely to regret sterilisation?
cards.a: Women under 30, those who have the procedure soon after delivery or during relationship stress, and those with few children are most likely to regret it. Careful counselling and a cooling-off period are essential, especially in younger women.

cards.q: How does vasectomy work and when is it effective?
cards.a: The vas deferens is cut or sealed so sperm cannot reach the ejaculate, but sperm already beyond the blockage take time to clear. It is not effective immediately, so backup contraception is needed until semen analysis confirms azoospermia.

cards.q: Why is vasectomy safer and more effective than tubal ligation?
cards.a: It is a minor outpatient procedure under local anaesthetic with fewer complications and a lower failure rate than tubal ligation, which needs general anaesthesia and abdominal surgery. When a couple is certain they want no more children, vasectomy is the preferred permanent method.

cards.q: How long must a man use backup contraception after vasectomy?
cards.a: Until a semen analysis, usually at 3 months and after at least 20 ejaculations, confirms no sperm. About 1 in 5 men still have sperm at 3 months, so the test, not the calendar alone, decides when backup can stop.

cards.q: Does vasectomy affect testosterone, erections or sexual function?
cards.a: No. It only blocks sperm transport; testosterone production, erections, ejaculation volume and libido are unchanged because the testes and hormone production are untouched. This myth is a common reason men decline the procedure.

cards.q: How effective are male condoms and what is their unique advantage?
cards.a: With typical use about 13 in 100 couples become pregnant in a year, but condoms are the only contraceptive method that also protects against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. They are therefore recommended for dual protection even with another method.

cards.q: What is dual protection and when should it be advised?
cards.a: Using condoms together with a highly effective method such as an IUD or implant, so the couple gets both pregnancy prevention and STI protection. It is advised for anyone with a new or multiple partners, or where STI risk is a concern.

cards.q: How do the diaphragm and cervical cap work, and what must be used with them?
cards.a: They are barrier devices placed in the vagina before sex to cover the cervix and block sperm, and they must be used with spermicide. They are less effective than hormonal methods and must be fitted, left in place for at least 6 hours after sex, and refitted after childbirth or weight change.

cards.q: Why is spermicide alone a poor choice for contraception?
cards.a: Used alone it has a typical-use failure rate of about 20 in 100 in a year because it does not reliably kill all sperm and is easily displaced. It is mainly useful as an adjunct to a barrier method such as a diaphragm.

cards.q: How do fertility awareness methods work, and who are they least suitable for?
cards.a: The woman tracks basal temperature, cervical mucus and cycle length to identify fertile days and avoids sex or uses condoms then. They are least suitable for women with irregular cycles, recent childbirth, or breastfeeding, because fertile days cannot be predicted reliably.

cards.q: How effective is withdrawal as contraception?
cards.a: With typical use about 20 in 100 couples become pregnant in a year, because pre-ejaculate can contain sperm and withdrawal timing is unreliable. It offers no STI protection and should not be relied on as a primary method.

cards.q: What are the three criteria for the lactational amenorrhea method (LAM)?
cards.a: The woman must be fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrheic, and less than 6 months postpartum. When all three are met it is over 98 percent effective, but as soon as any criterion fails another method is needed.

cards.q: Which contraceptive methods are safe during breastfeeding?
cards.a: Progestin-only pills, DMPA, the implant and IUDs are all safe because they contain no estrogen and do not reduce milk supply. Combined methods with estrogen are avoided in the early postpartum period, especially while breastfeeding.

cards.q: When can a COC be started after delivery, and why the delay?
cards.a: In non-breastfeeding women, not before 3 weeks postpartum, and not before 6 weeks if breastfeeding or other VTE risk factors are present. The early postpartum period carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism, and estrogen adds to that risk.

cards.q: When can an IUD be inserted after delivery?
cards.a: Immediately after delivery of the placenta, within 48 hours, or delayed until 4 weeks postpartum. Insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks is avoided because expulsion risk is highest then.

cards.q: Why are long-acting reversible methods recommended first-line for adolescents?
cards.a: Adolescents have the highest rates of pill non-adherence and unintended pregnancy, and IUDs and implants are over 99 percent effective without daily action. They are safe in adolescents, reversible, and do not require parental involvement in most settings.

cards.q: A 16-year-old asks for contraception and does not want her parents to know. What do you do?
cards.a: Provide confidential contraceptive care if she understands the decision, as adolescents can consent to contraception in most jurisdictions. Encourage her to involve a trusted adult, offer STI screening and condoms, and document the capacity assessment.

cards.q: A woman with epilepsy on carbamazepine needs contraception. Which method is best?
cards.a: A copper IUD or levonorgestrel IUD, because enzyme-inducing antiepileptics lower the levels of pills, implants and DMPA and can cause failure. IUDs act locally and are not affected by liver enzyme induction.

cards.q: Why is a copper IUD the safest choice for a woman on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics?
cards.a: It contains no hormones, so liver enzyme induction cannot reduce its effectiveness. Hormonal methods that rely on systemic hormone levels, including pills and implants, can all fail in this setting.

cards.q: Can a woman with diabetes without vascular complications use a COC?
cards.a: Yes, if she has no retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy or other vascular disease and her diabetes is well controlled. Estrogen is avoided only when vascular complications are present, because it adds cardiovascular and thrombotic risk.

cards.q: Why should a woman with diabetes and vascular disease avoid a COC?
cards.a: Vascular disease already raises the risk of arterial thrombosis, and estrogen adds further risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. A progestin-only method or an IUD is safer because it avoids estrogen.

cards.q: A woman has blood pressure of 150 over 95. Can she start a COC?
cards.a: No. Uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication to estrogen because COCs can raise blood pressure further and increase stroke and myocardial infarction risk. Control her blood pressure first, or offer a progestin-only method or IUD.

cards.q: A woman has migraine without aura. Can she use a COC?
cards.a: Yes, migraine without aura is not a contraindication to COCs in a non-smoker under 35. She should be counselled to report any new aura, worsening headaches or focal symptoms, and to stop estrogen if aura develops.

cards.q: Why does migraine with aura plus a COC raise stroke risk?
cards.a: Migraine with aura is independently associated with ischemic stroke, and estrogen increases clotting and vascular risk. The two together multiply the risk, so estrogen is avoided and a progestin-only or non-hormonal method is used instead.

cards.q: A woman with obesity wants contraception. Which methods are preferred and why?
cards.a: IUDs and implants are preferred because they remain highly effective regardless of BMI and do not add VTE risk. COCs are less attractive because obesity itself raises VTE risk and estrogen adds to it, and oral emergency contraception is less effective at higher weight.

cards.q: A woman with a BMI of 38 needs emergency contraception. What is the best option?
cards.a: A copper IUD, because its effectiveness is not reduced by body weight. Ulipristal is the next best oral option; levonorgestrel is least effective at this BMI.

cards.q: A 52-year-old perimenopausal woman with irregular periods asks when she can stop contraception. What do you tell her?
cards.a: She should continue contraception until 12 months of amenorrhea if she is over 50, or 24 months if under 50, because ovulation can still occur unpredictably in perimenopause. Pregnancy at this age is uncommon but possible and carries high risk.

cards.q: Why might a COC be useful for a perimenopausal woman?
cards.a: It regulates irregular bleeding, reduces hot flushes, protects bone density and provides contraception. It is suitable if she has no contraindications such as smoking over 35, hypertension or migraine with aura.

cards.q: A woman with a history of breast cancer needs contraception. What is the best option?
cards.a: A copper IUD, because it contains no hormones and cannot stimulate hormone-sensitive tissue. All hormonal methods, including COCs, POPs, DMPA, implants and levonorgestrel IUDs, are generally avoided in current or recent breast cancer.

cards.q: What do the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categories 1 to 4 mean?
cards.a: Category 1 means no restriction, category 2 means the advantages generally outweigh the risks, category 3 means the risks usually outweigh the advantages and specialist advice is needed, and category 4 means the method should not be used because the risk is unacceptable.

cards.q: What is the difference between MEC category 3 and category 4?
cards.a: Category 3 means the method can be used with careful judgement and specialist input because the risks usually outweigh the benefits, while category 4 means the method is absolutely contraindicated and must not be used. For example, smoking over 35 with a COC is category 4.

cards.q: A woman aged 40 who smokes wants a COC. What MEC category is this and what do you offer?
cards.a: This is MEC category 4, an unacceptable health risk, because smoking over age 35 plus estrogen markedly raises arterial thrombosis risk. Offer a progestin-only method or an IUD, and encourage smoking cessation.

cards.q: What is quick start contraception, and why is it useful?
cards.a: Starting a method on the day of the visit if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, rather than waiting for the next period. It improves uptake and continuation, and backup contraception is used for the first 7 days if she is not within the first 5 days of her cycle.

cards.q: A woman with an IUD cannot feel the strings. What should she do while waiting for review?
cards.a: Use condoms until the device position is confirmed, because the IUD may have been expelled and she may not be protected. She should also do a pregnancy test and seek review promptly rather than assuming the strings have simply retracted.

cards.q: A woman misses a COC pill and has unprotected sex. What backup advice do you give?
cards.a: Take the missed pill now, use condoms for the next 7 days, and consider emergency contraception if the missed pills were in week 1 or she missed two or more. Seven days of correct pill-taking are needed to re-establish ovulation suppression.

cards.q: How do you counsel a woman choosing between an implant and a COC?
cards.a: Explain that the implant is over 99 percent effective for 3 years without daily action and fertility returns immediately after removal, while the COC needs daily taking and is less forgiving of missed pills. The trade-off is unpredictable bleeding with the implant versus a regular monthly bleed with the COC.

cards.q: Why should condoms be recommended even when a woman uses an IUD?
cards.a: Because IUDs prevent pregnancy but give no protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Condoms are the only method that protects against STIs, so dual protection is advised with new or multiple partners.

Screening starts at age 21 with cytology (Pap) alone every 3 years, regardless of when she became sexually active. Starting earlier adds harms from treating transient HPV infections without benefit, because cervical cancer is rare before 21 and most HPV infections in young women clear on their own.
cards.q: A healthy 25-year-old woman with no prior abnormal Pap smears asks when cervical cancer screening should start. What do you tell her?

cards.a: Either Pap alone every 3 years, or Pap plus HPV co-testing every 5 years, or HPV testing alone every 5 years. After 30, HPV infections are more likely to persist, so adding HPV testing safely lengthens the interval because a negative HPV test predicts a very low cancer risk for years.
cards.q: A 32-year-old woman has had normal Pap smears. What is the recommended cervical cancer screening strategy for ages 30 to 65?

cards.a: No — screening can stop at 65 if she has had adequate prior screening (three consecutive negative Paps or two negative HPV-based tests in the last 10 years, most recent within 5 years) and no history of CIN 2 or worse in the last 25 years. Cervical cancer risk is very low after adequate negative screening, and continued testing mostly finds transient changes.
cards.q: A 68-year-old woman has had regular screening with negative results for the past 10 years. Does she still need cervical cancer screening?

cards.a: No routine Pap smears after total hysterectomy for benign disease with no history of CIN 2 or worse. Without a cervix there is essentially no cervical cancer risk, so screening offers no benefit.
cards.q: A 45-year-old woman had a total hysterectomy for benign fibroids with removal of the cervix. Does she need Pap smears?

cards.a: Pap smear every 6 months for the first year, then yearly if results stay normal. HIV impairs clearance of HPV, so dysplasia and cervical cancer develop faster and more often — she needs closer surveillance than an immunocompetent woman.
cards.q: A 28-year-old woman is HIV-positive with a normal Pap smear. How often should she have cervical screening?

cards.a: Yes — she needs continued surveillance with vaginal cuff cytology/HPV testing because she had cervical cancer. The 'stop after hysterectomy' rule applies only to benign indications with no history of high-grade dysplasia or cancer.
cards.q: A 35-year-old woman had a hysterectomy for cervical cancer 5 years ago. Does she still need vaginal cuff screening?

cards.a: No — women with a history of CIN 2, CIN 3, or adenocarcinoma in situ need at least 25 years of surveillance after treatment, even past age 65. Treated high-grade lesions carry a lasting risk of recurrence and cancer.
cards.q: A 40-year-old woman with a history of CIN 3 treated 10 years ago asks if she can stop screening at 65. What is the rule?

cards.a: Repeat Pap in 1 year (or repeat co-testing in 3 years per some guidelines; the classic Step 2 answer is repeat cytology in 1 year). ASC-US with negative HPV has a very low risk of high-grade disease, so surveillance is safe and avoids unnecessary colposcopy.
cards.q: A 26-year-old woman's Pap shows ASC-US and her reflex HPV test is negative. What is the next step?

cards.a: Colposcopy. ASC-US plus positive high-risk HPV means the atypia is likely HPV-driven and could hide CIN 2 or 3, so direct visualisation with biopsy is needed rather than watchful waiting.
cards.q: A 26-year-old woman's Pap shows ASC-US and her reflex HPV test is positive for high-risk HPV. What is the next step?

cards.a: Repeat Pap in 1 year, or colposcopy is also acceptable — but the preferred Step 2 answer is repeat cytology in 12 months. LSIL in a young woman usually reflects transient HPV infection that regresses, so observation avoids overtreatment.
cards.q: A 24-year-old woman's Pap shows LSIL. What is the next step?

cards.a: Colposcopy. In women over 25, LSIL is less likely to regress spontaneously and more likely to represent persistent HPV infection with underlying CIN, so biopsy-directed evaluation is warranted.
cards.q: A 45-year-old woman's Pap shows LSIL. What is the next step?

cards.a: Colposcopy with endocervical sampling. HSIL predicts CIN 2 or 3 in most cases and can hide invasive cancer, so immediate colposcopic evaluation with biopsy is required — never just repeat the Pap.
cards.q: A 30-year-old woman's Pap shows HSIL. What is the next step?

cards.a: Colposcopy. ASC-H carries a substantial risk of underlying CIN 2 or 3, similar to HSIL, so it cannot be managed with repeat cytology — direct biopsy is needed.
cards.q: A 38-year-old woman's Pap shows ASC-H (atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL). What is the next step?

cards.a: Colposcopy plus endocervical curettage, and endometrial sampling if she is over 35 or has abnormal bleeding. AGC can come from the cervix or the endometrium and can hide adenocarcinoma in situ or cancer, so both sites must be evaluated.
cards.q: A 50-year-old woman's Pap shows atypical glandular cells (AGC). What is the next step?

cards.a: Excisional treatment — LEEP (loop electrosurgical excision procedure) is preferred, or cold-knife cone if the lesion extends into the canal or adenocarcinoma in situ is suspected. CIN 2 is high-grade dysplasia with real progression risk, so it must be removed, and excision also gives a full histologic specimen to exclude invasion.
cards.q: Colposcopy in a 33-year-old with HSIL shows a visible lesion; biopsy shows CIN 2. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Close observation with colposcopy and Pap every 6 months is acceptable in young women, because CIN 2 often regresses and excision can increase the risk of preterm birth in future pregnancies. If it persists beyond 2 years or progresses to CIN 3, excision is done.
cards.q: A 24-year-old woman has biopsy-proven CIN 2. She wants children in the future. What management is acceptable?

cards.a: Observation with repeat Pap/HPV testing in 1 year — no treatment. CIN 1 is low-grade dysplasia from HPV that regresses in most women within 1 to 2 years, so treating it would cause harm without benefit.
cards.q: A 29-year-old woman has biopsy-proven CIN 1. What is the management?

cards.a: Excisional treatment with LEEP or cold-knife cone. CIN 3 is carcinoma in situ — the immediate precursor to invasive cancer — and it rarely regresses, so it must be completely removed.
cards.q: A 41-year-old woman has CIN 3 on biopsy. What is the treatment?

cards.a: HPV-based testing at 6 months, then annually; if negative, every 3 years. HPV testing after treatment is the most sensitive way to detect residual or recurrent disease, and a negative test predicts a very low recurrence risk.
cards.q: After LEEP for CIN 3, what is the recommended follow-up?

cards.a: Colposcopy without endocervical curettage and without biopsy unless invasive cancer is suspected. Pregnancy changes the cervix and makes biopsy risky (bleeding), and CIN does not progress to invasive cancer quickly, so diagnosis is confirmed but definitive treatment waits until after delivery.
cards.q: A 36-year-old pregnant woman at 16 weeks has a Pap showing HSIL. What is the next step?

cards.a: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV, especially types 16 and 18. HPV oncoproteins E6 and E7 inactivate the tumour suppressors p53 and Rb, allowing uncontrolled cell growth — which is why nearly all cervical cancers are HPV-related.
cards.q: A 55-year-old woman has postcoital bleeding and a visible exophytic mass on the cervix. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most common cause of this cancer?

cards.a: Often asymptomatic and found on screening — when symptomatic, the classic features are postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. The cervix is visible on exam, so cancer here often announces itself with bleeding after intercourse before it causes pain.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of early cervical cancer?

cards.a: Tumour spread to the pelvic sidewall obstructing the ureter (causing hydronephrosis) and compressing pelvic veins/lymphatics (causing leg oedema). Cervical cancer spreads locally into the parametrium and pelvic sidewall, and ureteral obstruction is a classic late complication — it is even part of staging.
cards.q: A woman with locally advanced cervical cancer has leg swelling and a non-functioning kidney on imaging. What explains this?

cards.a: Radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection, or definitive chemoradiation — both are curative for early-stage disease. Surgery is favoured in young women to preserve ovarian function and avoid radiation damage to the vagina and bladder.
cards.q: A 48-year-old woman with stage IB1 cervical cancer (small tumour confined to the cervix) asks about treatment. What is the standard option?

cards.a: Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin-based chemotherapy plus pelvic radiation). Once cancer has spread beyond the cervix into the parametrium, surgery alone cannot clear it, and chemoradiation is the standard curative treatment for locally advanced disease.
cards.q: A woman with stage IIB cervical cancer (parametrial involvement, not to the pelvic wall) is best treated with what?

cards.a: Stage at diagnosis, especially lymph node involvement. Early-stage disease confined to the cervix is highly curable, while nodal spread and parametrial invasion sharply lower survival — which is why screening that catches pre-invasive disease matters so much.
cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in cervical cancer?

cards.a: Radical trachelectomy — removal of the cervix with preservation of the uterus — plus pelvic lymph node dissection. It is an option only for small, early-stage tumours with negative nodes, because it removes the cancer while leaving the uterus so pregnancy remains possible.
cards.q: A 30-year-old woman with cervical cancer wants to preserve fertility. She has a tumour under 2 cm confined to the cervix. What procedure may be offered?

cards.a: HPV 18 is more associated with adenocarcinoma than HPV 16. Adenocarcinoma arises in the endocervical canal, so it is harder to sample on a Pap smear and is more often missed by cytology alone — one reason HPV testing improves detection.
cards.q: A woman is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the cervix. Which HPV type is most associated, and how does screening differ from squamous cancer?

cards.a: Punch biopsy of the visible lesion — the diagnosis is made by tissue biopsy, not by repeating the Pap. A visible mass with malignant cytology needs histologic confirmation and staging before any treatment is planned.
cards.q: A 60-year-old woman has a Pap showing malignant cells and a friable cervical mass. What is the next best step in her workup?

cards.a: Postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecologic cancer, and any bleeding after menopause must be evaluated for it first — it is cancer until proven otherwise.
cards.q: A 63-year-old woman, 12 years postmenopausal, has vaginal bleeding for 2 weeks. What is the most important diagnosis to rule out?

cards.a: Transvaginal ultrasound measuring endometrial thickness, followed by endometrial biopsy if the stripe is thickened (over 4 to 5 mm) or if bleeding persists. Ultrasound is a good first triage test, but biopsy is the diagnostic test — a thin stripe makes cancer unlikely.
cards.q: A 62-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding. What is the first step in evaluation?

cards.a: Endometrial biopsy (pipelle). It is the diagnostic test of choice — quick, office-based, and highly sensitive for endometrial cancer, which is usually a diffuse process that a blind biopsy can sample.
cards.q: A 58-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding and an endometrial stripe of 12 mm on ultrasound. What is the next step?

cards.a: Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, plus surgical staging with lymph node assessment. Most endometrial cancers are caught early, and surgery alone is often curative.
cards.q: A 65-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage I endometrioid endometrial cancer. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Unopposed estrogen — estrogen without progesterone. Examples include estrogen-only hormone replacement, obesity (adipose tissue converts androgens to estrogen), anovulation (PCOS), and estrogen-secreting tumours. Estrogen drives endometrial proliferation, and progesterone normally opposes it, so unopposed estrogen is the key risk factor.
cards.q: A woman with obesity and PCOS develops endometrial cancer. What is the shared risk factor linking her conditions to this cancer?

cards.a: Combined estrogen-progesterone oral contraceptives and progestin therapy. Progesterone opposes estrogen-driven proliferation, which is why combined pills are protective and progestins are used to treat endometrial hyperplasia.
cards.q: Which hormonal therapy protects against endometrial cancer?

cards.a: Heavy, irregular bleeding with intermenstrual spotting in a woman in her 40s or 50s, often with obesity or anovulation. The bleeding comes from a thickened, hyperplastic endometrium that sheds irregularly — and the same unopposed estrogen can progress to cancer.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of endometrial hyperplasia?

cards.a: Endometrial biopsy first — age over 45 with abnormal uterine bleeding requires tissue sampling to exclude hyperplasia or cancer. Ultrasound can be done, but it does not replace biopsy in this age group.
cards.q: A 47-year-old woman has heavy, irregular menstrual bleeding for 6 months. What is the first diagnostic step?

cards.a: Treat with progestin therapy (oral or levonorgestrel IUD) and repeat biopsy in 3 to 6 months. Simple hyperplasia without atypia rarely progresses to cancer, so hormonal treatment that opposes estrogen is safe and effective — surgery is not needed.
cards.q: Endometrial biopsy shows simple hyperplasia without atypia in a 46-year-old woman. What is the management?

cards.a: Hysterectomy. Atypical hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia) is a direct precursor to endometrial cancer and progresses in a substantial proportion of cases, so definitive treatment is removal of the uterus.
cards.q: Endometrial biopsy shows complex atypical hyperplasia in a 52-year-old woman. What is the management?

cards.a: Abnormal uterine bleeding, heavy or irregular periods, and in premenopausal women it can also cause infertility. Submucosal fibroids distort the cavity and disrupt bleeding; subserosal fibroids more often cause bulk symptoms like urinary frequency.
cards.q: A 38-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and a uterus enlarged to 14-week size. What is the most likely cause, and what is the classic bleeding pattern of uterine fibroids?

cards.a: Pelvic ultrasound — the first test to confirm fibroids, define their location, and assess the endometrium. MRI is reserved for surgical planning or when ultrasound is unclear.
cards.q: A 40-year-old woman has heavy periods and a palpable pelvic mass. What is the first imaging test?

cards.a: The levonorgestrel IUD is first-line medical therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding from fibroids or adenomyosis when fertility is not immediately desired — it reduces bleeding markedly by thinning the endometrium locally. NSAIDs and tranexamic acid are also options; hysterectomy is definitive but last-line.
cards.q: A 42-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding from small fibroids wants medical treatment and does not want surgery. What is the first-line option?

cards.a: Rapidly enlarging uterus, especially after menopause — leiomyosarcoma is rare but aggressive, and postmenopausal growth of a 'fibroid' is the classic red flag. A fibroid that grows after menopause should not be assumed benign.
cards.q: A 60-year-old woman has a pelvic mass thought to be a fibroid that has doubled in size in 6 months. What diagnosis must be considered?

cards.a: Anovulatory bleeding — common at the extremes of reproductive age (adolescents and perimenopausal women). Immature or failing hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis causes estrogen without ovulation and without progesterone, so the endometrium grows and sheds irregularly. Diagnosis is by exclusion after ruling out pregnancy, structural causes, and coagulopathy.
cards.q: A 16-year-old girl has irregular, heavy periods since menarche. Pregnancy test is negative and exam is normal. What is the most likely cause?

cards.a: Von Willebrand disease — the most common inherited bleeding disorder, and a common cause of heavy menstrual bleeding in adolescents. Always ask about easy bruising, nosebleeds, and bleeding after dental work or surgery in a teenager with heavy periods.
cards.q: A 14-year-old girl has heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and a history of frequent nosebleeds and bruising. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

cards.a: Bloody, foul-smelling vaginal discharge and postcoital bleeding in a woman whose cancer is often diagnosed on biopsy after an abnormal Pap. Vaginal cancer is rare, and most vaginal cancers are squamous cell carcinoma related to HPV.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of primary vaginal cancer?

cards.a: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina (or cervix), classically in young women whose mothers took diethylstilbestrol (DES) during pregnancy. DES exposure in utero causes vaginal adenosis, which can transform into clear cell cancer — a classic Step 2 association.
cards.q: A 22-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding and is found to have clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina. What in-utero exposure explains this?

cards.a: Vaginal adenosis — glandular (columnar) epithelium in the vagina instead of squamous epithelium. It is the hallmark finding of in-utero DES exposure and the precursor lesion for clear cell adenocarcinoma.
cards.q: What is the most common finding on exam in a woman exposed to DES in utero?

cards.a: Vulvar itching and a white, crinkly, parchment-like plaque — lichen sclerosus. It most often affects postmenopausal women, causes intense pruritus, and is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva, so any suspicious area needs biopsy.
cards.q: A 68-year-old woman has severe vulvar itching and a white, thin, crinkly patch on the vulva. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: High-potency topical corticosteroids (clobetasol). They control the inflammation and itching of lichen sclerosus and reduce the risk of scarring; any persistent ulcer or mass still needs biopsy to exclude cancer.
cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for vulvar lichen sclerosus?

cards.a: A painless, ulcerated or raised lesion on the vulva in an older woman, often with itching. Most vulvar cancers are squamous cell carcinoma, and HPV-related tumours occur in younger women while lichen sclerosus-related tumours occur in older women.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of vulvar cancer?

cards.a: Biopsy of the lesion. Vulvar cancer is diagnosed by tissue biopsy, not by Pap or imaging — any persistent vulvar ulcer or mass in an older woman must be biopsied.
cards.q: A 70-year-old woman has a non-healing ulcer on the vulva. What is the next step?

cards.a: Wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy for early-stage disease. Radical vulvectomy is reserved for larger or multifocal tumours; early disease can be treated with more limited surgery plus nodal assessment.
cards.q: A woman is diagnosed with stage I vulvar squamous cell carcinoma. What is the treatment?

cards.a: HPV 16 and 18 — the same high-risk types that cause cervical cancer. Vaccination against HPV therefore also protects against vulvar, vaginal, and anal cancers.
cards.q: Which HPV types cause most HPV-related vulvar cancers?

cards.a: Postmenopausal bleeding and a polypoid mass protruding from the vagina. Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) is a rare vaginal cancer of young girls, presenting with a grape-like mass — a classic paediatric association.
cards.q: A 4-year-old girl has vaginal bleeding and a grape-like mass protruding from the vagina. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Ovarian cancer is usually diagnosed late because early symptoms are vague — bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary frequency, and weight loss. The classic Step 2 presentation is a postmenopausal woman with months of bloating and a pelvic mass, often with ascites.
cards.q: A 62-year-old woman has 3 months of abdominal bloating, early satiety, and weight loss. Exam shows a pelvic mass and shifting dullness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler is the first imaging test to characterise an adnexal mass (solid vs cystic, septations, vascularity). CT of the abdomen and pelvis is used for staging once cancer is suspected, but ultrasound comes first.
cards.q: A 55-year-old woman has a palpable adnexal mass. What is the first imaging test?

cards.a: CA-125 is elevated in most epithelial ovarian cancers, but it is not a screening test — it is too non-specific (elevated in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, and other cancers) and too insensitive for early disease. It is used to follow response to treatment and detect recurrence.
cards.q: A 60-year-old woman with suspected ovarian cancer has a CA-125 of 450 U/mL. Is CA-125 a screening test for ovarian cancer?

cards.a: Epithelial ovarian cancer, most commonly high-grade serous carcinoma — it accounts for the large majority of ovarian cancers and is the most lethal gynaecologic cancer because it presents late with peritoneal spread.
cards.q: What is the most common type of ovarian cancer?

cards.a: Cytoreductive (debulking) surgery to remove as much tumour as possible, followed by platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin plus paclitaxel). The amount of residual disease after surgery is the strongest predictor of survival, so maximal debulking matters.
cards.q: A 63-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage III ovarian cancer. What is the standard treatment?

cards.a: No routine screening is recommended for average-risk women. Ultrasound and CA-125 have not been shown to reduce ovarian cancer deaths and cause many false positives leading to unnecessary surgery, so screening is only offered in high-risk (BRCA) women.
cards.q: A healthy 50-year-old woman with no family history asks about ovarian cancer screening. What do you tell her?

cards.a: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations — they greatly increase the risk of ovarian and breast cancer. A woman with a BRCA1 mutation has a lifetime ovarian cancer risk high enough that risk-reducing surgery is recommended.
cards.q: A 35-year-old woman has a mother and sister who both had ovarian cancer. What genetic mutation should be tested for?

cards.a: Risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing is complete, usually between ages 35 and 40 for BRCA1. Removing the ovaries and tubes removes the tissue where cancer arises, and is the most effective prevention — screening alone does not prevent ovarian cancer.
cards.q: A 38-year-old BRCA1-positive woman has completed childbearing. What is the recommended risk-reducing measure for ovarian cancer?

cards.a: Oral contraceptives — they suppress ovulation, and each year of use lowers ovarian cancer risk. This is the 'incessant ovulation' theory: repeated ovulation damages the ovarian surface epithelium, so suppressing it is protective. Multiparity and breastfeeding are also protective.
cards.q: Which medication lowers the risk of ovarian cancer?

cards.a: Torsion — a twisted ovary cuts off its blood supply, causing sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, nausea, and vomiting. It is a surgical emergency: the ovary must be untwisted promptly to save it, and the diagnosis is supported by ultrasound with Doppler showing absent flow, but imaging should not delay surgery when suspicion is high.
cards.q: A 28-year-old woman has sudden severe right lower quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting. Ultrasound shows a 7 cm ovarian cyst with absent Doppler flow. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: A complex adnexal mass with solid components in a postmenopausal woman — any complex or solid mass after menopause is cancer until proven otherwise and needs surgical evaluation by a gynaecologic oncologist. Functional cysts essentially do not occur after menopause.
cards.q: A 66-year-old woman has a 6 cm complex adnexal mass with solid areas. What is the concern and the next step?

cards.a: Serum beta-hCG, AFP, and LDH — germ cell tumours (dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumour, choriocarcinoma) secrete these markers. Germ cell tumours are the most common ovarian malignancy in young women and are highly curable, so marking them before surgery matters.
cards.q: A 22-year-old woman has a pelvic mass. Which tumour markers should be checked before surgery?

cards.a: Dysgerminoma — the most common malignant germ cell tumour, equivalent to seminoma in men. It is highly sensitive to chemotherapy and has an excellent prognosis, even when advanced.
cards.q: A 20-year-old woman has an ovarian mass and a markedly elevated LDH. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Yolk sac tumour — it secretes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). A young woman with a pelvic mass and a very high AFP has a yolk sac tumour until proven otherwise.
cards.q: A 19-year-old woman has an ovarian mass and an AFP of 800 ng/mL. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Meigs syndrome — the triad of a benign ovarian fibroma, ascites, and pleural effusion (usually right-sided). Removing the fibroma resolves both the ascites and the effusion, which distinguishes it from malignant ascites.
cards.q: A 58-year-old woman has a pelvic mass, ascites, and a right pleural effusion. Surgery removes a benign ovarian fibroma and the fluid resolves. What is this syndrome?

cards.a: Krükenberg tumour — metastatic signet-ring cell carcinoma to the ovaries, usually from a gastric primary. Bilateral solid ovarian masses in a woman with a known GI cancer should raise this diagnosis.
cards.q: A woman with gastric cancer develops bilateral solid ovarian masses. What is this called?

cards.a: Mucinous cystadenoma or mucinous cystadenocarcinoma — large mucin-filled cysts can cause pseudomyxoma peritonei, with mucinous ascites throughout the abdomen. The classic presentation is a very large, multilocular cystic mass.
cards.q: A woman has a huge multilocular cystic ovarian mass with mucinous ascites. What is the likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Struma ovarii — a teratoma made of thyroid tissue that can cause hyperthyroidism. Mature cystic teratomas (dermoid cysts) are the most common benign ovarian tumour in young women and can contain hair, teeth, and fat.
cards.q: A 30-year-old woman has a pelvic mass and new hyperthyroidism with no goitre. Imaging shows a dermoid cyst. What explains the hyperthyroidism?

cards.a: Mammography starting at age 40, every 2 years until age 74 (USPSTF), or annually from 40 to 44 then every 2 years (ACS). The exact interval is debated, but the Step 2 standard is to start at 40 — earlier screening is for high-risk women only.
cards.q: A healthy 42-year-old woman with no family history asks when breast cancer screening should start. What do you tell her?

cards.a: Continue screening as long as she is in good health with a life expectancy over 10 years. Age alone is not a reason to stop — health and life expectancy decide.
cards.q: A 76-year-old woman in good health asks if she should stop mammography. What do you tell her?

cards.a: Mammography with tomosynthesis plus breast MRI, starting at age 30 (or 10 years before the youngest affected relative). BRCA carriers have a very high lifetime breast cancer risk, and MRI is more sensitive than mammography in dense young breasts.
cards.q: A 32-year-old BRCA1-positive woman asks about breast cancer screening. What is recommended?

cards.a: A new, painless, hard, irregular, non-mobile breast lump — the classic presentation of breast cancer. Most breast cancers are found by the patient herself as a lump; pain is uncommon and does not rule out cancer.
cards.q: What is the classic presentation of breast cancer?

cards.a: Bilateral mammogram first, then ultrasound to distinguish solid from cystic. A palpable lump in a woman over 30 needs imaging before biopsy — mammography can reveal other lesions and calcifications, and ultrasound tells you if it is a simple cyst.
cards.q: A 55-year-old woman has a painless hard breast lump. What is the first imaging test?

cards.a: Core needle biopsy — it gives a histologic diagnosis plus receptor status (ER, PR, HER2), which determines treatment. Fine-needle aspiration gives cells only and cannot reliably give receptor status, so core biopsy is preferred.
cards.q: A woman has a suspicious breast mass on mammography. What is the diagnostic test of choice?

cards.a: The most likely diagnosis is a fibroadenoma — a benign, mobile, rubbery, well-circumscribed lump, the most common benign breast tumour in young women. It does not increase cancer risk and can be observed after confirmation.
cards.q: A 22-year-old woman has a smooth, mobile, rubbery 2 cm breast lump. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cards.a: A simple cyst — the most common cause of a breast lump in premenopausal women. Aspiration relieves it and confirms the diagnosis if the fluid is non-bloody and the lump disappears; bloody fluid or a residual mass needs biopsy.
cards.q: A 45-year-old woman has a smooth, tender, mobile breast lump that fluctuates with her cycle. Ultrasound shows a simple cyst. What is the diagnosis and management?

cards.a: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) — malignant cells confined to the ducts without invasion. It is usually found as microcalcifications on mammography, and is treated with lumpectomy plus radiation (or mastectomy for extensive disease).
cards.q: A woman's mammogram shows clustered microcalcifications. Biopsy shows malignant cells confined to the ducts with no invasion. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Invasive ductal carcinoma — the most common type of breast cancer, accounting for about 80 percent of invasive cancers. Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common and is more often bilateral and multifocal.
cards.q: What is the most common type of invasive breast cancer?

cards.a: Peau d'orange (orange-peel skin), nipple retraction, and bloody nipple discharge are red flags for cancer. Peau d'orange comes from lymphatic obstruction by tumour, and nipple retraction from tumour pulling on Cooper ligaments.
cards.q: A woman has a breast lump with dimpled skin and a retracted nipple. What do these findings suggest?

cards.a: Inflammatory breast cancer — it presents with erythema, warmth, oedema, and peau d'orange over a large area, mimicking mastitis, but without fever and without response to antibiotics. Any 'mastitis' that does not improve with antibiotics in a non-lactating woman needs biopsy.
cards.q: A 50-year-old non-lactating woman has a red, warm, swollen breast that has not improved after 2 weeks of antibiotics. What diagnosis must be ruled out?

cards.a: Mastitis is treated with antibiotics and continued breastfeeding (emptying the breast helps); a breast abscess needs drainage. Mastitis is common in lactating women from Staphylococcus aureus, presenting with a painful, erythematous, tender breast with fever.
cards.q: A 28-year-old breastfeeding woman has a painful, red, hot area of her breast with fever. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Paget disease of the breast — an eczematous, scaly, crusted nipple lesion that is almost always associated with underlying ductal carcinoma. Any persistent nipple eczema that does not respond to topical steroids needs biopsy.
cards.q: A 55-year-old woman has a scaly, itchy, crusted nipple that has not improved with topical steroids for 3 months. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations — the most important inherited cause of breast cancer. BRCA1 cancers are often triple-negative (ER, PR, and HER2 negative), while BRCA2 cancers are more often hormone-receptor positive.
cards.q: A 40-year-old woman has breast cancer and a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer. What genetic test is most important?

cards.a: A positive sentinel lymph node — nodal status is the most important prognostic factor in early breast cancer. Tumour size, grade, and receptor status also matter, but nodal involvement most strongly predicts recurrence and survival.
cards.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in early-stage breast cancer?

cards.a: Tamoxifen — it blocks estrogen receptors and is used in premenopausal women with ER-positive cancer. In postmenopausal women, aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole) are preferred because they block estrogen production in peripheral tissues.
cards.q: A premenopausal woman has ER-positive breast cancer. Which hormonal therapy is used?

cards.a: Trastuzumab — a monoclonal antibody against HER2, used in HER2-positive breast cancer. HER2-positive tumours are aggressive, but targeted therapy has markedly improved their prognosis.
cards.q: A woman's breast cancer is HER2-positive. Which targeted therapy is added to chemotherapy?

cards.a: Lumpectomy with radiation is equivalent to mastectomy in survival for early-stage breast cancer, provided clear margins can be achieved and radiation can be given. Breast-conserving surgery is preferred when feasible because it preserves the breast without worsening survival.
cards.q: A woman with a 2 cm breast cancer asks whether she must have a mastectomy. What do you tell her?

cards.a: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 cause most cervical cancers and precancers; low-risk types 6 and 11 cause genital warts (condyloma acuminata) and low-grade lesions. Knowing the type matters because only high-risk types drive cancer.
cards.q: Which HPV types cause cervical cancer, and which cause genital warts?

cards.a: Yes — the HPV vaccine is recommended for everyone aged 9 to 26, and can be given up to age 45 after shared decision-making. It protects against future infection with the types in the vaccine, even though it does not clear an existing infection — so sexually active women still benefit.
cards.q: A 24-year-old sexually active woman asks if the HPV vaccine will still help her. What do you tell her?

cards.a: The 9-valent HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9), given as 2 doses if started before age 15 and 3 doses if started at 15 or older. It covers HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58 — the types responsible for most cervical cancers and genital warts.
cards.q: Which HPV vaccine is used, and how many doses are given?

cards.a: Genital warts (condyloma acuminata) — soft, cauliflower-like growths caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11. They are not precancerous, but they are sexually transmitted and can recur; treatment is topical (podophyllin, imiquimod) or ablative.
cards.q: A 23-year-old woman has multiple soft, cauliflower-like lesions on the vulva. What is the diagnosis and the cause?

cards.a: No — the vaccine does not treat existing HPV infection or CIN, so she still needs colposcopy and treatment of her lesion. The vaccine prevents new infections with vaccine types, and she may still benefit from it, but it is not a treatment.
cards.q: A 30-year-old woman with CIN 2 asks if the HPV vaccine will cure her dysplasia. What do you tell her?

cards.a: Routine Pap screening is still needed. The vaccine covers the most common cancer-causing HPV types but not all of them, so vaccinated women can still develop cervical cancer and must be screened on the same schedule.
cards.q: A 21-year-old woman who completed the HPV vaccine series asks if she still needs Pap smears. What do you tell her?
